question.text: A river has a width of 30 m and flows with a speed of 4 m/s. A boatman can row at a speed of 5 m/s in still water.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Sketch the velocity vector diagram corresponding to crossing the river in the minimum possible time. Calculate this minimum duration, the resultant speed of the boatman relative to the ground, and the distance drifted downstream.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine whether the boatman can arrive at a point directly opposite the initial location on the opposite bank. If it is possible, provide the velocity diagram, the direction in which the boat must be steered, and the time taken for this crossing.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the total time required for the boatman to travel a distance of 10 m upstream and then row back to the starting location.

conditions: speed of boatman relative to water = 5 m/s

solution.approach: For shortest time row straight across; for reaching the point directly opposite, angle the boat upstream so the along-river components cancel.

steps.text: For the shortest time, row the boat straight across the river, perpendicular to the bank, using the full rowing speed to cross.
The net velocity of the boatman is the vector sum of the across and along components, and the drift is the along part times the time.
To land directly opposite, the boat must be rowed upstream at an angle θ so its along-river component cancels the river current.
The resulting net speed across the river is the rowing speed times cos θ, and the crossing time follows.
Rowing 10 m up the stream and back uses the speeds relative to the ground on each leg, since the boat moves along the river direction.
Add the two times together for the total time up and back.

final_answer.value: (a) t = 6 s, net velocity ≈ 6.4 m/s, drift = 24 m; (b) yes, row at 53° to the perpendicular (upstream) with t = 10 s; (c) t ≈ 11.1 s

common_mistakes.text: Using 5 + 4 = 9 m/s for the upstream-and-back leg speeds instead of 5 − 4 and 5 + 4 separately gives a wrong total time.
Taking the net velocity for shortest-time crossing as only 5 m/s, ignoring the river current, gives a wrong resultant speed.

question.text: From the same location, two objects are launched straight upward with an identical launch speed v₀. If the second object is released a time interval t₀ s following the first, find the time elapsed from the projection of the first object until they meet.
conditions: launched vertically upwards from the same spot
second object launched t₀ s after the first

solution.approach: Write the height of each body as a function of time measured from the first launch, with the second body's clock starting t₀ later, and set the two heights equal.

steps.text: Measure time t from the first launch. Its height above the ground is v₀t − ½gt².
The second body is launched t₀ later, so for t ≥ t₀ its height uses time (t − t₀).
Set the two heights equal, since the bodies meet at that height.
steps.equation: v₀t − ½gt² = v₀(t − t₀) − ½g(t − t₀)²

steps.text: Expand and simplify; the squared terms combine using the difference of squares, and t₀ cancels from both sides.
steps.equation: v₀t₀ = ½g t₀(2t − t₀) → v₀ = ½g(2t − t₀)

steps.text: Solve for t, the time after the first launch at which the bodies meet.

final_answer.value: The bodies meet at t = v₀/g + t₀/2 measured from the first launch, which is v₀/g − t₀/2 measured from the second launch.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the bodies meet exactly halfway through the time gap, at t = t₀/2 after the first launch, which ignores the actual rise and fall of each body under gravity.

question.text: During the time interval 2 s ≤ t ≤ 6 s, an object moves along a straight path such that its velocity v and acceleration a (in m/s²) satisfy the relation v = 4/a m/s. Given that the velocity of the object is v = 6 m/s at the instant t = 2 s, calculate its acceleration at t = 3 s.
conditions: valid for time interval 2 s ≤ t ≤ 6 s

solution.approach: Write acceleration as dv/dt = 4/v, separate variables and integrate to get v(t), then compute a = 4/v at t = 3 s.

steps.text: Write acceleration as dv/dt and set it equal to the given relation.
Separate the variables and integrate both sides.
Use v = 6 m/s at t = 2 s to find the constant C.
Find v at t = 3 s from v²/2 = 4t + 10.
Find the acceleration at t = 3 s using a = 4/v.
steps.why_this_step: The acceleration is not constant here since it depends on v, so it must be re-evaluated at the new speed.

common_mistakes.text: Using the velocity given at t = 2 s directly in a = 4/v, getting a = 4/6 = 0.667 m/s² instead of solving for v at t = 3 s.
Writing the left side of ∫v dv as v instead of v²/2, so that v = 4t + C, gives v = 10 m/s at t = 3 s and a = 0.4 m/s².

question.text:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion and Reason. Choose the correct option from the given choices.

Assertion: A particle moving with constant acceleration cannot have its average velocity equal to zero over any duration.
Reason: For the average velocity of a moving object to vanish, its non-zero velocity must not stay unchanging.

options.1: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.2: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
options.4: Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

solution.approach: Test the claim with a ball thrown up and caught at the same point; the average velocity over the trip is zero even though the acceleration is uniform throughout.

steps.text: Take a ball thrown upward at 20 m/s under gravity g = 10 m/s², a constant, uniform acceleration throughout its flight.
Find the total time of flight, up and back down to the same starting height.
Find the net displacement over this time; it returns exactly to the starting point.
The average velocity is this net displacement divided by the time, giving zero even though the acceleration was uniform and nonzero throughout, so the Assertion is false.

The Reason correctly states that average velocity can only be zero when the velocity does not stay a fixed nonzero value throughout, which is a true condition, so the Reason is true even though the Assertion is false.

final_answer.value: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming uniform acceleration always produces a changing, nonzero average velocity, missing the case of a body that returns to its starting point.

question.text: Consider the following claim: An object undergoing projectile motion travels along a two-dimensional path while experiencing a uniform acceleration. State whether this proposition is true or false.
conditions: uniform acceleration (acceleration due to gravity is constant)

solution.approach: Check both parts of the statement against the definition of projectile motion: its plane of motion and its acceleration.

steps.text: A projectile moves in a vertical plane, so its motion needs two coordinates: it is two-dimensional.
Its only acceleration is gravity, which stays constant in magnitude and direction through the whole flight.
Both parts of the statement match the physics of projectile motion, so the statement is true.

common_mistakes.text: Believing the acceleration changes because the velocity direction keeps changing during the flight, when only the velocity changes, not the acceleration.

question.text: An aircraft travels directly from location P to location Q, situated 1000 km to the north. A steady wind moves eastward at 200 km/h, while the aircraft maintains a speed of 500 km/h relative to the surrounding air.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the heading direction the pilot must steer to arrive at Q.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Calculate the duration needed to complete the flight from P to Q.

conditions: straight-line path from P to Q
distance from P to Q is 1000 km due north
wind velocity is 200 km/h due east
speed of aircraft relative to air is 500 km/h
resultant velocity of aircraft relative to ground is directed due north

solution.approach: The plane must head upwind of north so that the wind's eastward push is cancelled by a westward component of its airspeed, leaving a net northward velocity.

steps.text: Let θ be the angle west of north the pilot heads; the westward component of airspeed must cancel the eastward wind.
Solve for θ.
Find the resulting northward component of velocity.
Find the time to cover 1000 km at this northward speed.

final_answer.value: (a) the pilot should head about 23.6° west of north. (b) time taken ≈ 2.18 h (about 2 h 11 min).

common_mistakes.text: Adding the airspeed and wind speed directly to get a resultant of 700 km/h, giving a wrong time of 1000/700 ≈ 1.43 h.
Ignoring the wind entirely and using the plane's airspeed alone, giving time = 1000/500 = 2 h.

question.text: A body travels in a straight line along the x-axis. When t = 0 s, the location of the body is x = −4 m. The velocity of the body varies with time according to v = 8 − 2t, with v given in m/s and t in s.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: How many distinct instances does the body find itself 8 m away from the origin?

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine the exact values of time at which these occurrences take place.

conditions: initial position x = −4 m at t = 0
velocity v = 8 − 2t with v in m/s and t in s

figure.description: A schematic showing the x-axis with marks at −8 m, −4 m, 0 m, and +8 m. At t = 0, the object starts at x = −4 m with a rightward velocity of 8 m/s and a constant leftward acceleration of 2 m/s². The trajectory illustrates the object moving rightward across x = +8 m at time t₁, halting at v = 0, reversing direction to pass x = +8 m again at time t₂, and eventually reaching x = −8 m at time t₃.

solution.approach: Integrate the velocity equation to get x(t), then solve x = 8 and x = −8 separately, keeping only the positive-time roots.

steps.text: Integrate the given velocity to get the x-coordinate, using x = −4 m at t = 0.
Set x(t) = 8 and solve the quadratic for t.
Set x(t) = −8 and solve the quadratic for t, keeping only the positive root.
steps.equation: −4+8t−t² = −8 → t²−8t−4=0 → t = 4+2√5 ≈ 8.47 s (the other root is negative)

steps.text: Count all the positive times found: the particle is at a distance of 8 m from the origin three times.

common_mistakes.text: Discarding the negative-x case x = −8 entirely and reporting only 2 times, missing that the particle turns back and passes x = −8 later.
Keeping the negative root t = 4−2√5 ≈ −0.47 s from the x = −8 case as a valid time, which is not physical since t must be positive.

question.text: Starting from rest at ground level, a rocket is launched vertically with an effective upward acceleration of 4 m/s². Its engine shuts down after 5 s when all fuel is consumed, after which the rocket moves under the influence of gravity alone (taking g = 10 m/s²). It continues upward while slowing down until momentarily coming to rest at its peak altitude, and subsequently free-falls back to the ground. Sketch the velocity-time and displacement-time curves for the entire duration of the flight.
conditions: uniform upward acceleration of 4 m/s² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5 s
fuel runs out at t = 5 s
motion under gravity with g = 10 m/s² downward for t > 5 s
velocity equals zero at maximum height

figure.description:
Two graphs are displayed:
1. Velocity-time (v in m/s vs t in s): A straight line segment ascends from the origin (0, 0) to point A at (5, 20), followed by a straight line segment with a steeper negative slope passing through point B at (7, 0) and terminating at point C at (10.7, −37.4).
2. Displacement-time (s in m vs t in s): A parabolic curve opening upward extends from (0, 0) to point A at (5, 50), connects to a parabolic curve opening downward that peaks at point B at (7, 70), and returns to the time axis at point C at (10.7, 0).

solution.approach: Split the journey into three phases of constant acceleration, powered rise, coasting rise, and free fall, and find the velocity and displacement at the end of each.

steps.text: Phase 1, powered flight for 5 s with acceleration 4 m/s² from rest: find the velocity and height reached.
Phase 2, after the fuel ends the rocket decelerates under gravity alone until its velocity reaches zero; find the time taken and the extra height gained.
steps.equation: Δt = 20/10 = 2 s (total t = 7 s), Δs = 20²/(2×10) = 20 m (total s = 70 m)

steps.text: Phase 3, the rocket falls freely from rest at 70 m under gravity; find the time to reach the ground.

The v-t graph rises from 0 to 20 m/s over 0–5 s, then falls to about −37.4 m/s by t ≈ 10.74 s, crossing zero at t = 7 s. The s-t graph rises from 0 to 50 m over 0–5 s, peaks at 70 m at t = 7 s, then falls to 0 at t ≈ 10.74 s.

final_answer.value: Rises to v = 20 m/s and s = 50 m at t = 5 s; coasts to the highest point s = 70 m at t = 7 s; falls back to the ground at t ≈ 10.74 s, landing at about 37.4 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Using the powered-phase acceleration of 4 m/s² instead of g = 10 m/s² for the coasting and falling phases, which changes the peak height and total time.
Forgetting to add the fall time to the 7 s already elapsed, reporting the total flight time as √14 ≈ 3.74 s instead of about 10.74 s.

question.text: The velocity of an object travelling along a straight line varies with time as v = (3 + 6t + 9t²) cm/s, where t is in seconds. Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The acceleration of the object at t = 3 s.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Its displacement during the time interval from t = 5 s to t = 8 s.

solution.approach: Differentiate the velocity for acceleration and integrate it between the two times for displacement.

steps.text: Differentiate v with respect to time to get the acceleration.
Substitute t = 3 s.
Integrate v with respect to time from t = 5 s to t = 8 s to get the displacement.
Evaluate the integral at the two limits and subtract.

common_mistakes.text: Differentiating 9t² as 9t instead of 18t gives an acceleration of 33 cm/s² at t = 3 s instead of 60 cm/s².
Subtracting the velocity at t = 5 s from the velocity at t = 8 s instead of integrating gives 369 cm instead of 1287 cm.

question.text: The position–time (x–t) plots for two bodies, A and B, traveling along the x-axis are straight lines. At time t = 0 s, body A is located at x = 10 m while body B is at the origin (x = 0 m). At t = 5 s, both bodies reach x = 12 m. Determine the velocity of body A relative to body B.
conditions: position of A at t = 0 s is 10 m
position of B at t = 0 s is 0 m
both particles are at x = 12 m at t = 5 s

figure.description: A position versus time (x–t) graph showing position x in meters on the vertical axis and time t in seconds on the horizontal axis. Particle A's straight-line trajectory begins at (0 s, 10 m), while particle B's straight-line trajectory begins at the origin (0 s, 0 m). The two lines intersect at the coordinates (5 s, 12 m).

solution.approach: The slope of each x-t line is that particle's velocity, and the relative velocity is the difference of the two velocities.

steps.text: Find the velocity of A from the slope of its line using the two given points, (t = 0, x = 10 m) and (t = 5 s, x = 12 m).
Find the velocity of B from the slope of its line using the two given points, (t = 0, x = 0) and (t = 5 s, x = 12 m).
Velocity of A with respect to B is the vector difference of the two velocities.
steps.why_this_step: Both lines are straight, so each slope is a constant velocity, and the relative velocity is also constant.

common_mistakes.text: Subtracting in the wrong order, v_B − v_A, gives +2 m/s instead of −2 m/s.
Reading A's slope from the intersection point without the 10 m starting offset, as 12/5 = 2.4 m/s, gives v_AB = 0 instead of −2 m/s.

question.text: An object travels along a straight line such that its x-coordinate varies with time according to the equation x = (2 + t² + 2t³), where x is expressed in metres and time t is in seconds. Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the location from which the object began its motion,

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the initial velocity of the object,

parts.label: c
parts.asks: the acceleration of the object at t = 2 s.

solution.approach: Read the starting position directly from x at t = 0, then differentiate x once and twice for velocity and acceleration.

steps.text: The particle's starting position is x at t = 0.
Differentiate x with respect to time to get the velocity, then substitute t = 0.
Differentiate v with respect to time to get the acceleration, then substitute t = 2 s.

common_mistakes.text: Reporting the velocity at t = 2 s, which is 28 m/s, instead of differentiating a second time for the acceleration, which is 26 m/s².

question.text: An object having a mass of 10 kg moves with an initial speed of 10 ms⁻¹. It is subjected to a forward force described by 3t² and a constant resistive force of 32 N. What will be the velocity of the object at t = 5 s?

solution.approach: Write the net force as a function of time, divide by mass to get acceleration, and integrate over the 5 seconds to add on to the initial speed.

steps.text: Write the net force on the body: the time-varying force minus the constant opposing force.
Divide by the mass to get the acceleration as a function of time.
Integrate the acceleration from 0 to 5 s to get the change in velocity.
Add this change to the initial speed to get the velocity at t = 5 s.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting to add the initial speed of 10 ms⁻¹ and reporting only the magnitude of the change in velocity gives 3.5 ms⁻¹.

question.text: A body is dropped from an elevation of 125 m starting with zero initial velocity. Compute its average velocity for the entire fall until reaching the ground. (Use g = 10 m/s²).

solution.approach: Find the time to fall through the height using free fall kinematics, then divide the height by that time.

steps.text: Write the height fallen from rest as a function of time and solve for the time to reach the ground.
Substitute the height and g to find the time of fall.
Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the factor 2 in h = ½gt² and using t = √(h/g) gives a time of about 3.54 s and an average velocity of about 35.4 m/s, which is wrong.

question.text: Two vehicles, A and B, begin traveling at the same moment along a straight horizontal path in the identical forward direction. At time t = 0, vehicle A is located 10 m behind vehicle B. Vehicle A accelerates from rest at a uniform rate of a = 4 m/s², whereas vehicle B proceeds at a steady speed of v = 1 m/s. Calculate the time elapsed before vehicle A catches up to vehicle B.
conditions: motion along a straight line in the same direction
vehicles begin motion simultaneously at t = 0
initial separation is 10 m with car A behind car B
car A starts from rest with uniform acceleration a = 4 m/s²
car B travels with constant velocity v = 1 m/s

solution.approach: Write the position of each car as a function of time from a common origin and solve for the time at which the two positions become equal.

steps.text: Place car A at the origin at t = 0, with car B 10 m ahead of it. Car A starts from rest with constant acceleration; car B moves at constant velocity.
Car A overtakes car B when their positions are equal.
Solve the quadratic equation for t.
Keep only the positive root, since time cannot be negative.

common_mistakes.text: Keeping the negative root t = −2 s instead of discarding it can lead to picking the wrong sign in the final answer.
Writing car A's position as 4t² instead of 2t² by forgetting the half in ½at² gives a wrong quadratic and a wrong time.

question.text: The velocity vector of a moving body at time t is expressed as v = (2 î + 2t ĵ) m/s. Assuming the body starts from the origin at t = 0, calculate its acceleration vector and displacement vector at t = 1 s. Furthermore, explain whether the kinematic relation v = u + at is applicable to this motion.
conditions: velocity given by v = (2 î + 2t ĵ) m/s

solution.approach: Differentiate v to check whether the acceleration is constant, then integrate v for the displacement.

steps.text: Differentiate v with respect to time to get the acceleration.
The acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction for every t, even though v itself changes direction with time.
Integrate v with respect to time from 0 to 1 s to get the displacement.
Since the acceleration is constant, v = u + at can be applied; checking it at t = 1 s confirms this matches v(1).
steps.equation: u + at = 2î + 2ĵ = v(1), so yes, v = u + at applies

final_answer.value: a = 2ĵ m/s²; displacement = (2î + ĵ) m; yes, v = u + at can be applied because a is constant

common_mistakes.text: Assuming v = u + at cannot be applied because the velocity's direction changes with time, without checking whether the acceleration itself is constant.

question.text: From a height of 12 m, a ball is projected straight up with an initial speed of 18 m/s. Exactly at this moment, an open-platform lift crosses the 5 m mark while ascending at a steady speed of 2 m/s. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², calculate:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the time and location where the ball encounters the platform,

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the velocity of the ball measured relative to the platform upon collision.

conditions: ball projected vertically upward from y = 12 m with v₀ = 18 m/s
elevator ascends at constant velocity 2 m/s from y = 5 m at t = 0

solution.approach: Write the ball's height under gravity and the elevator's height at constant speed as functions of time, set them equal to find when they meet, then find their relative velocity.

steps.text: Write the ball's height using free-fall kinematics and the elevator's height using constant velocity.
Set the two heights equal and simplify to a quadratic in t.
Solve the quadratic and keep the positive root.
Find the meeting height using the elevator's equation.
Find the relative velocity of the ball with respect to the elevator at this instant.

final_answer.value: (a) the ball meets the elevator at t ≈ 3.66 s, at a height of about 12.31 m. (b) relative velocity of the ball with respect to the elevator ≈ 19.83 m/s, directed downward.

common_mistakes.text: Solving for when the ball returns to the elevator's starting height of 5 m, ignoring that the elevator itself keeps moving up, which gives the wrong time t ≈ 4.03 s.
Assuming the ball is still moving upward at the meeting instant instead of already falling, giving a wrong relative velocity of about 15.83 m/s instead of 19.83 m/s.

question.text: A particle travels within the x-y plane such that its position coordinates at instant t are given by (2t, t²). Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the equation of the particle's trajectory,

parts.label: b
parts.asks: its velocity at time t, and

parts.label: c
parts.asks: its acceleration at any instant t.

solution.approach: Eliminate t between the two coordinates to get the path, then differentiate each coordinate once for velocity and again for acceleration.

steps.text: The coordinates are x = 2t and y = t². Solve the first for t and substitute into the second.
This is the equation of the path traced by the particle.
Differentiate x and y with respect to t to get the velocity components.
steps.equation: vₓ = dx/dt = 2 ms⁻¹, v_y = dy/dt = 2t ms⁻¹

steps.text: The velocity vector and its magnitude follow from these components.
Differentiate the velocity components again to get the acceleration.
steps.equation: aₓ = dvₓ/dt = 0, a_y = dv_y/dt = 2 ms⁻², so acceleration is 2 ms⁻² along y, constant for all t

final_answer.value: (a) y = x²/4 (a parabola), (b) velocity has components vₓ = 2 ms⁻¹, v_y = 2t ms⁻¹, magnitude 2√(1+t²) ms⁻¹, (c) acceleration is constant, 2 ms⁻² along y, at every time t

common_mistakes.text: Writing the trajectory as y = t² without eliminating t, which leaves the path expressed in terms of time instead of in terms of x and y.

question.text: The position of an object traveling along a straight path varies with time according to the relation x = 32t − (8/3)t³, where the coordinate x is in metres and time t is in seconds. Determine its acceleration at the moment it momentarily comes to a stop.
conditions: x is in metres and t in seconds
evaluated at the instant the particle is at rest

solution.approach: Differentiate the position function to get velocity, find the time the particle is at rest, then differentiate again to get acceleration at that time.

steps.text: Differentiate the position function to get the velocity.
Set the velocity to zero and solve for the physically valid (positive) time.
Differentiate the velocity to get acceleration, then evaluate it at t = 2 s.

common_mistakes.text: Solving 32 − 8t² = 0 and taking the negative root t = −2 s instead of the physical t = 2 s, giving a(−2) = 32 ms⁻².

question.text: A particle travels along a straight horizontal line with its velocity expressed as v = (3t² − 6t) m/s, where t is the time in seconds. Starting from the origin at t = 0, calculate the following for the duration between t = 0 and t = 3.5 s:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The total distance covered by the particle

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The average velocity of the particle

parts.label: c
parts.asks: The average speed of the particle

conditions: time interval from t = 0 to t = 3.5 s

solution.approach: Split the motion where velocity reverses sign, integrate to get position, add distances in each part for total distance, and use net displacement for average velocity.

steps.text: Set v = 3t² − 6t equal to zero to find when the particle reverses direction.
Integrate v with respect to t, taking the particle at the origin at t = 0, to get its position.
Find the position at t = 0, t = 2 s and t = 3.5 s.
From t = 0 to t = 2 s the particle moves from 0 to −4 m; from t = 2 s to t = 3.5 s it moves from −4 m to 6.125 m. Add these distances.
steps.why_this_step: Total distance adds the length travelled in each leg of the trip, even where the particle doubles back.

steps.text: Average velocity uses net displacement over the interval; average speed uses total distance over the interval.
steps.equation: average velocity = 6.125/3.5 = 1.75 m/s, average speed = 14.125/3.5 ≈ 4.04 m/s

final_answer.value: distance travelled = 14.125 m, average velocity = 1.75 m/s, average speed ≈ 4.04 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Taking the net displacement x(3.5) − x(0) = 6.125 m as the total distance, missing that the particle reverses direction at t = 2 s and travels back and forth.
Reporting average speed as equal to average velocity, 1.75 m/s, without separating distance from displacement.

concept_tags: velocity as a function of time

question.text: At the same instant, two bodies, A and B, travel along a straight path in an identical direction. Particle A has an initial speed of 3 m/s and maintains a constant acceleration of 1 m/s², while particle B has an initial speed of 1 m/s and an acceleration of 2 m/s². If particle A begins at a position 10 m behind particle B, determine the closest distance of approach between the two particles.
conditions: motion along a straight line in the same direction
constant acceleration of A is 1 m/s²
constant acceleration of B is 2 m/s²
initial speed of A is 3 m/s
initial speed of B is 1 m/s
initial separation is 10 m with A behind B

solution.approach: Write the separation between B and A as a function of time and minimize it with calculus.

steps.text: Write each particle's position from its own start, then the separation as B's position minus A's position, starting from the given 10 m gap.
Set the derivative of the separation to zero to find the time of closest approach.
Substitute t = 2 s back into the separation to get the minimum distance.
steps.why_this_step: The second derivative of s(t) is positive, so this turning point is a minimum, not a maximum.

common_mistakes.text: Using only the initial speeds and ignoring the accelerations suggests the gap keeps closing forever, missing that B's larger acceleration makes B faster than A after t = 2 s, so the gap widens again.

question.text: An object possesses an initial velocity v₀ = 10 ms⁻¹ and is subjected to a deceleration of magnitude 0.2v², where v represents its instantaneous velocity. What will be the velocity of the object at t = 2 s?

solution.approach: Write the retardation as dv/dt = −0.2v² and separate the variables to find v as a function of t.

steps.text: Write the equation of motion using the given retardation.
Separate the variables and integrate from v₀ = 10 at t = 0 to v at time t.
Rearrange to express 1/v.
Substitute v₀ = 10 and t = 2 s.
Take the reciprocal to find the velocity after 2 s.

question.text: A particle, initially at rest, begins rectilinear motion with a uniform acceleration. When a duration t₀ has elapsed, the direction of this acceleration is reversed while its magnitude remains unchanged. Find the total elapsed time T from the start until the particle arrives back at its starting point.
conditions: acceleration reverses sign at t = t₀
returns to the starting point at total time T

solution.approach: Split the motion into the first phase of duration t₀ and a second phase with reversed acceleration, then find when the total displacement returns to zero.

steps.text: In the first phase, from rest with acceleration a for time t₀, find the velocity and displacement reached.
In the second phase the acceleration becomes −a. Let τ be the time measured after t₀, and write the total displacement at that point.
Set the total displacement to zero and solve the resulting quadratic for τ.
steps.equation: ½t₀² + t₀τ − ½τ² = 0 → τ² − 2t₀τ − t₀² = 0 → τ = t₀(1 + √2)

steps.text: Add τ to t₀ for the total time T at which the point mass is back at the start.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the second phase exactly mirrors the first and the point mass returns at T = 2t₀ ignores that the mass keeps moving forward for a while in the second phase before it turns back.

question.text: The position-time (x–t) graph of an object moving in one dimension consists of straight-line segments passing through the points (0 s, 0 m), (2.5 s, 50 m), (7.5 s, 50 m), (10.0 s, 100 m), and (15.0 s, 0 m). Using this information, calculate:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the average velocity over the time interval from 0 to 10 s

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the instantaneous velocity at the time instants t = 2 s, t = 5 s, t = 8 s, and t = 12 s

conditions: x = 50 m at t = 2.5 s and t = 7.5 s

figure.description: A graph of position x (in m) plotted against time t (in s). The curve starts at (0, 0), rises with a constant positive slope to (2.5, 50), stays horizontal at x = 50 until t = 7.5, continues upward linearly to (10.0, 100), and then descends linearly to meet the time axis at (15.0, 0).

solution.approach: Find the average velocity from the net displacement over 0 to 10 s, then read the slope of the graph at each given time for the instantaneous velocities.

steps.text: Average velocity is the net displacement divided by the time interval, from t = 0 to t = 10 s.
At t = 2 s the particle is on the rising segment from (0,0) to (2.5,50); its slope is the velocity.
At t = 5 s the particle is on the flat segment from t = 2.5 s to t = 7.5 s, where x stays at 50 m.
At t = 8 s the particle is on the segment rising from (7.5,50) to (10,100); its slope is the velocity.
At t = 12 s the particle is on the falling segment from (10,100) to (15,0); its slope is the velocity.

common_mistakes.text: Carrying the slope from the first rising segment forward and reporting v(5) = 20 m/s, without noticing the graph is flat between t = 2.5 s and t = 7.5 s.
Reporting the speed 20 m/s at t = 12 s without the negative sign that shows the particle is moving back towards the origin.

question.text: An elevator begins moving upward from a stationary state, with its acceleration changing over time as shown in the given graph. The acceleration is 2 ms⁻² between t = 0 and t = 4 s, remains 0 from t = 4 s to t = 8 s, and is −2 ms⁻² between t = 8 s and t = 12 s. Determine the total vertical displacement of the elevator from its initial level by the time it stops.
conditions: starts from rest (initial velocity is zero)
acceleration a = 2 ms⁻² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 s
acceleration a = 0 for 4 s < t ≤ 8 s
acceleration a = −2 ms⁻² for 8 s < t ≤ 12 s

figure.description: An acceleration-time graph showing acceleration a in ms⁻² on the vertical axis and time t in s on the horizontal axis. A horizontal line segment extends from t = 0 to t = 4 s at a = 2 ms⁻². The curve lies on the time axis (a = 0) from t = 4 s to t = 8 s. A horizontal line segment extends from t = 8 s to t = 12 s at a = −2 ms⁻².

solution.approach: Read the acceleration in each of the three time segments, find the velocity at each segment boundary, and add the distance covered in each segment.

steps.text: From t = 0 to 4 s, acceleration is 2 ms⁻² from rest. Find the velocity and distance covered by the end of this segment.
From t = 4 to 8 s, acceleration is 0, so the lift moves at the constant velocity 8 ms⁻¹. Find the distance covered.
From t = 8 to 12 s, acceleration is −2 ms⁻². Check that the lift comes to rest exactly at t = 12 s.
Find the distance covered while the velocity falls from 8 ms⁻¹ to 0 over this last segment.
Add the three distances to get the total height above the starting point.

common_mistakes.text: Treating zero acceleration in the middle segment as zero velocity, so skipping the 32 m travelled at constant speed and adding only the first and last segments: 16 + 16 = 32 m.

question.text: A particle moving in the x-y plane experiences a time-dependent acceleration described by a = (2t î + 3t² ĵ) m/s². At the moment t = 0, it begins moving from the origin with an initial velocity of 2 m/s directed along the positive x-axis. Determine the velocity vector and the position coordinates of the particle at t = 1 s.

solution.approach: Integrate the acceleration once for velocity, adding the initial velocity, then integrate again for position, starting from the origin.

steps.text: Integrate a with respect to time and add the initial velocity to get v(t).
Substitute t = 1 s.
Integrate v with respect to time, starting from the origin, to get the coordinates.
Substitute t = 1 s to get the coordinates.

common_mistakes.text: Integrating the acceleration for velocity without adding the initial velocity of 2 m/s along the x-axis gives v(1) = (î + ĵ) m/s instead of (3î + ĵ) m/s.
Integrating the acceleration components twice without carrying the initial velocity into the position integral gives an x-coordinate of 1/3 m instead of 7/3 m.

question.text: An object is thrown straight up into the air with a starting speed of 40 m/s. Determine both its total displacement and the overall distance it travels during the first 6 s of its flight. (Use g = 10 m/s²)

solution.approach: Check whether the particle has already turned back within the 6 s, then add the upward and downward distances separately for the distance covered.

steps.text: Displacement in 6 s follows directly from the standard equation of motion, taking upward as positive.
Find the time taken to reach the highest point, where the velocity becomes zero.
Since 4 s is less than 6 s, the particle has already turned around and is falling back for the last 2 s; find the maximum height it reached.
Find how far it falls back down in the remaining time after reaching the top.
The displacement is the height reached minus the distance fallen back, matching the direct calculation, while the total distance covered is the height reached plus the distance fallen back.
steps.why_this_step: Distance keeps adding up regardless of direction, while displacement is the net change in position.

common_mistakes.text: Reporting the distance as equal to the displacement, 60 m, without checking that the particle reversed direction before 6 s had passed.
Assuming the particle has returned all the way to the starting point by 6 s and taking the distance as twice the maximum height, 160 m.

question.text: An object travels along a circular path having a radius of 4 cm at a uniform speed of 1 cm/s. Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The time period of revolution for the object.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The magnitudes of the average speed, average velocity, and average acceleration over the duration from t = 0 to t = T/4, where T denotes the time period.

conditions: time interval from t = 0 to t = T/4

solution.approach: Use circumference over speed for the period, then work out the distance, the chord, and the velocity change over a quarter turn.

steps.text: The time period is the circumference divided by the constant speed.
From t = 0 to t = T/4 the particle covers a quarter of the circle, in a time of T/4.
Since the speed never changes, the average speed over any interval equals this constant speed.
The displacement is the straight chord joining the start and end points, which are 90° apart on the circle, so the average velocity is this chord divided by the time.
steps.equation: displacement = r√2 = 4√2 cm, average velocity = 4√2/(2π) ≈ 0.90 cm/s

steps.text: Over the quarter turn the velocity direction rotates by 90° while its magnitude stays at 1 cm/s, giving a velocity-vector change of v√2; the average acceleration is this change divided by the time.
steps.why_this_step: The velocity vectors at the two instants are perpendicular, so their difference has magnitude v√2, not zero.

final_answer.value: (a) T = 8π s ≈ 25.13 s. (b) average speed = 1 cm/s, average velocity ≈ 0.90 cm/s, average acceleration ≈ 0.23 cm/s²

common_mistakes.text: Subtracting the two speed values instead of the velocity vectors, 1 − 1 = 0, and concluding the average acceleration is zero, which ignores the change in direction.
Using the quarter-circle arc length as the displacement instead of the straight chord, which gives an average velocity equal to the average speed, 1 cm/s.

question.text:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion and Reason. Choose the appropriate option that describes them.

Assertion: Based on the formula a = v(dv/ds), whenever the velocity of a body equals zero, its acceleration must likewise vanish.
Reason: The quantity a defined in this expression represents the instantaneous acceleration.

options.1: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.2: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
options.4: Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

solution.approach: Test the claim with free fall from rest: at the starting instant velocity is zero, but the acceleration a = v dv/ds still gives a finite, nonzero value.

steps.text: For free fall from rest through a height s, the speed follows v² = 2gs, so v = √(2gs) and dv/ds = g/v.
Form the product a = v dv/ds; the v in front cancels the v in the denominator of dv/ds, leaving a constant, even as v approaches zero near the start.
steps.why_this_step: As s becomes very small, v also becomes very small, but dv/ds grows without bound, so the product v dv/ds stays finite and equal to g rather than going to zero.

steps.text: This shows a = v dv/ds does not force acceleration to zero when velocity is zero; the Assertion's conclusion is false, while the Reason, that a in this formula is the instantaneous acceleration, is a true definition on its own and does not justify the false conclusion.

final_answer.value: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Substituting v = 0 directly into a = v dv/ds and reading off a = 0, without checking that dv/ds can be infinite at that point.

question.text: A particle travels along a straight path such that its speed v decreases as a linear function of position s, starting at 20 m/s when s = 0 and reaching zero at s = 30 m. Find the acceleration of the body at the position s = 15 m.
conditions: velocity varies linearly with displacement s

solution.approach: Write velocity as a linear function of displacement, then use a = v(dv/ds) at s = 15 m.

steps.text: Velocity falls linearly from 20 m/s at s = 0 to 0 at s = 30 m; write v as a function of s.
Differentiate v with respect to s; the slope is constant.
Find v at s = 15 m.
Use a = v(dv/ds) with v = 10 m/s and dv/ds = −2/3 to find the acceleration.

common_mistakes.text: Using the starting velocity 20 m/s instead of the velocity at s = 15 m, giving a = 20 × (−2/3) = −13.3 m/s².
Dropping the negative sign on the slope and writing a = 10 × (2/3) = 6.67 m/s².

question.text: The position of an object travelling across the xy-plane is given as a function of time by x = 2t² and y = t³, where coordinates x and y are measured in metres and time t is in seconds. Determine the average acceleration of the object over the duration from t = 0 to t = 2 s.
conditions: time interval from t = 0 to t = 2 s

solution.approach: Differentiate the coordinates to get the velocity components, then find the average acceleration from the change in velocity over the time interval.

steps.text: Differentiate x and y with respect to time to get the velocity components.
Evaluate the velocity components at t = 0 and t = 2 s.
steps.equation: at t=0: vₓ=0, v_y=0; at t=2: vₓ=8 m/s, v_y=12 m/s

steps.text: Divide the change in each velocity component by the time interval.
Combine the components as a vector and find the magnitude.

common_mistakes.text: Finding the instantaneous acceleration aₓ=4, a_y=6t at t=2 s instead of averaging, giving (4î + 12ĵ) m/s².

question.text: A vehicle A moves with an acceleration of 2 m/s² towards the east, while a vehicle B accelerates at 4 m/s² towards the north. Determine the relative acceleration of vehicle B as observed from vehicle A.
conditions: car A accelerates at 2 m/s² due east
car B accelerates at 4 m/s² due north
motion occurs in a horizontal plane

solution.approach: Relative acceleration is the vector difference of the two accelerations, found by adding the perpendicular east and north components.

steps.text: Write the two accelerations as vectors along east and north.
Apply the relative acceleration formula.
Find the magnitude of the resultant.
Find the direction using the two perpendicular components, −2 (west) and 4 (north).
steps.equation: tan α = 4/2 = 2 → α = tan⁻¹(2) ≈ 63.4°, measured from west towards north

final_answer.value: a_(B/A) = 2√5 m/s² ≈ 4.47 m/s², directed about 63.4° north of west (equivalently about 26.6° west of north)

common_mistakes.text: Adding a_A and a_B instead of subtracting gives a_(B/A) = (2î + 4ĵ), a different direction, north-east instead of north-west.
Computing the magnitude as 4 − 2 = 2 m/s² by treating the two accelerations as if they were along the same line, ignoring that they are perpendicular.

question.text: A particle travels along the x-axis such that its position as a function of time is given by the relation x = 20 + t³ − 12t, where all quantities are expressed in SI units.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the position and velocity of the particle at t = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: State whether the particle moves with uniform acceleration or not.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Calculate the location of the particle at the instant its velocity drops to zero.

solution.approach: Differentiate the position equation to get velocity, differentiate again to get acceleration, then apply the conditions asked.

steps.text: Write the velocity and acceleration by differentiating x with respect to time.
steps.equation: x = 20 + t³ − 12t, v = dx/dt = 3t² − 12, a = dv/dt = 6t

steps.text: Substitute t = 0 into x and v.
Check whether acceleration is constant.
steps.why_this_step: Uniformly accelerated motion needs a constant acceleration; here a depends on t, so it is not.

steps.text: Set v = 0 and solve for t.
steps.equation: 3t² − 12 = 0 → t² = 4 → t = 2 s (t = −2 s rejected, time cannot be negative)

steps.text: Substitute t = 2 s into x to get the position where velocity is zero.

final_answer.value: (a) x(0) = 20 m, v(0) = −12 m/s; (b) not uniformly accelerated, since a = 6t is not constant; (c) x = 4 m when v = 0

common_mistakes.text: Taking both roots t = 2 s and t = −2 s as valid positions gives an extra wrong answer x(−2) = 36 m for a time before the motion starts.
Assuming acceleration is constant just because it comes from a smooth equation leads to wrongly calling the motion uniformly accelerated.

question.text:
An object moves along the x-axis such that its speed remains constant within each given time period as follows:
• From 0 s to 2 s, its speed is 2 m/s
• From 2 s to 5 s, its speed is 3 m/s
• From 5 s to 10 s, its speed is 4 m/s
• From 10 s to 15 s, its speed is 2 m/s

Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The overall distance covered during the entire motion.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The average speed of the object over the 15 s interval.

conditions: speed is constant during each specified time interval

solution.approach: Multiply each interval's speed by its duration to get the distance in that interval, add them for the total distance, then divide by the total time.

steps.text: Find the distance covered in each time interval by multiplying speed by the interval duration.
Add the four distances to get the total distance.
Divide the total distance by the total time of 15 s to get the average speed.

final_answer.value: total distance = 43 m, average speed ≈ 2.87 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Taking the plain average of the four speed values instead of the distance-weighted average, giving (2+3+4+2)/4 = 2.75 m/s.

question.text: A body travels along a straight path with its position given by the relation x = (2t − 3)², in which x denotes metres and t denotes seconds. Calculate:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: its position, velocity, and acceleration at the instant t = 2 s.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: its velocity when it passes through the origin.

solution.approach: Differentiate x twice for velocity and acceleration, then find the velocity when x itself is zero.

steps.text: Differentiate x with respect to time to get the velocity, using the chain rule.
Differentiate v with respect to time to get the acceleration.
Substitute t = 2 s into x, v and a.
Set x = 0 to find when the particle is at the origin, then find the velocity there.

final_answer.value: (a) x = 1 m, v = 4 m/s, a = 8 m/s²; (b) velocity at origin = 0 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Differentiating (2t−3)² without the chain-rule factor of 2 from the inner 2t gives v = 2(2t−3), which is 2 m/s at t = 2 s instead of 4 m/s.
Reading 'at origin' as t = 0 instead of x = 0 gives a velocity of −12 m/s instead of 0 m/s.

question.text: Consider an object undergoing rectilinear motion with constant acceleration. At instant t = 0, its velocity equals v₁, while at instant t = t, its velocity reaches v₂. The claim states that its mean velocity over this duration is (v₁ + v₂)/2. State whether this statement is true or false.
conditions: velocity at t = t is v₂

solution.approach: For uniform acceleration, velocity is a linear function of time, so its average over any interval equals the average of the endpoint values.

steps.text: Write velocity as a linear function of time for uniform acceleration.
Average velocity over 0 to t is the mean value of this linear function.
Since v₂ = v₁ + at, substitute at = v₂ − v₁ into the average. This gives the stated formula, so the statement is true.

question.text: The velocity-time relation of an object traveling along a straight path is represented in the given plot. Initially, at time t = 0, the object is situated at a distance of 10 m from the reference mean position. Determine the following:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The acceleration of the object at the time instants t = 1 s, t = 3 s, and t = 9 s.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The location of the object relative to the reference mean position at t = 10 s.

parts.label: c
parts.asks:
The displacement-time (s-t) expressions for the periods:
(i) 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s
(ii) 4 s ≤ t ≤ 8 s

conditions: initial displacement from mean position at t = 0 is 10 m

figure.description: A graph of velocity v (in m/s) on the vertical axis against time t (in s) on the horizontal axis. The curve begins at (0 s, 0 m/s), increases uniformly to (2 s, 10 m/s), remains constant at 10 m/s until t = 4 s, decreases linearly passing through (6 s, 0 m/s) to reach (8 s, −10 m/s), and finally increases linearly to end at (10 s, 0 m/s).

solution.approach: Read acceleration from the slope of each v-t segment, and get position by adding the signed area under v-t to the given starting position.

steps.text: Find the slope of the v-t line at t = 1 s, 3 s and 9 s from the segment each falls in.
steps.equation: a(1 s) = 5 m/s² (0–2 s segment), a(3 s) = 0 (2–4 s segment, constant v), a(9 s) = 5 m/s² (8–10 s segment)

steps.text: Start the position at s = 10 m at t = 0 and add the area under v-t up to each breakpoint to find s at t = 10 s.
For 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s, v = 5t; integrate to get s(t).
For 4 s ≤ t ≤ 8 s, v = 10 − 5(t − 4), starting from s(4) = 40 m; integrate and collect terms in t.

common_mistakes.text: Reading the acceleration at t = 3 s as nonzero, forgetting that a straight horizontal segment of the v-t graph means zero acceleration.
Writing the s-t equation for 4 s ≤ t ≤ 8 s starting the position from zero instead of from s(4) = 40 m, the value already reached by that time.

question.text:
Assertion: An object's speed can reduce even while the acceleration it experiences is growing.
Reason: A reduction in speed takes place whenever the acceleration is positive.

options.1: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.2: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
options.4: Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

conditions: speed is the magnitude of velocity

solution.approach: Test the claim with a particle whose acceleration opposes its velocity and grows in magnitude; speed falls as the acceleration's magnitude rises, but here the acceleration is negative, not positive.

steps.text: Take a particle moving in the positive direction with velocity v(t) = 5 − t²/2, so its acceleration is a(t) = −t.
Check the speed and the size of the acceleration at increasing times while v stays positive.
steps.equation: at t = 1 s: v = 4.5 m/s, |a| = 1 m/s²; at t = 2 s: v = 3.0 m/s, |a| = 2 m/s²

steps.text: The speed has fallen from 4.5 m/s to 3.0 m/s while the size of the acceleration has grown from 1 m/s² to 2 m/s², so the Assertion is true; but in this example the acceleration is negative, opposing the velocity, not positive as the Reason claims.
steps.why_this_step: Speed falls whenever acceleration opposes velocity, whatever the sign of either one on its own; a positive acceleration acting on a positive velocity would instead increase the speed.

steps.text: The Assertion is true, but the Reason gives an incomplete and, in this example, incorrect condition, so the Reason is false.

final_answer.value: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

common_mistakes.text: Treating 'acceleration is positive' as the general condition for slowing down, without checking that it actually depends on the acceleration opposing the velocity's direction.

concept_tags: relative direction of velocity and acceleration

question.text: A roofless lift moves upwards at a steady rate of 10 m/s. While standing inside it at an altitude of 10 m above ground level, a person launches a ball straight upwards with a speed of 30 m/s relative to the lift. Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the highest elevation reached by the ball from the ground,

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the time elapsed until the ball returns to the lift,

parts.label: c
parts.asks: the additional time needed for the ball to strike the ground after passing the lift on its descent.

conditions: lift moves upward at constant speed v = 10 m/s
launch height h = 10 m above the ground
speed of ball relative to lift = 30 m/s upward
motion under gravity with g = 9.8 m/s² or 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Add the elevator's velocity to the ball's relative velocity to get its ground-frame velocity, then use straight-line motion under g = 10 m/s² for all three parts.

steps.text: The elevator ascends at constant speed, so it has zero acceleration. The ball's velocity in the ground frame at launch is the elevator's velocity plus the ball's velocity relative to the elevator.
For part (a), find the extra height the ball rises above the launch point using v² = u² − 2g(rise), then add the launch height h = 10 m above the ground.
steps.equation: rise = u²/(2g) = 1600/20 = 80 m, max height = 10 + 80 = 90 m

steps.text: For part (b), measure both positions from the launch point: the ball's height is y_ball(t) = ut − ½gt², and the elevator's floor height is y_elev(t) = 10t. Set them equal to find when the ball meets the elevator again.
For part (c), the ground is 10 m below the launch point, so solve y_ball(t) = −10 for the time the ball lands, then subtract the meeting time found in part (b).
steps.why_this_step: The quadratic has two roots, 4 − 3√2 ≈ −0.24 s and 4 + 3√2 ≈ 8.24 s. The negative root is a time before the throw, so the landing time is t = 4 + 3√2 ≈ 8.24 s.

steps.text: Subtract the meeting time from the landing time to get the time taken after crossing the elevator.

final_answer.value: (a) 90 m above the ground, (b) 6 s, (c) (3√2 − 2) s ≈ 2.24 s

common_mistakes.text: Using only the 30 m/s relative velocity as the ball's ground-frame speed, forgetting to add the elevator's 10 m/s, gives a maximum height of 55 m instead of 90 m.
Treating the elevator as stationary and setting the ball's height above the launch point to zero gives a meeting time of 8 s instead of the correct 6 s.

question.text: Determine whether the following claim is correct or incorrect: An object's average speed is invariably identical to the absolute value of its average velocity.
conditions: motion over a finite time interval

solution.approach: Compare the definitions: average speed uses total distance, average velocity uses total displacement, and distance can exceed displacement.

steps.text: Write the two definitions over the same time interval.
steps.equation: average speed = distance/time, average velocity = displacement/time

steps.text: Distance travelled is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement, with equality only for one-directional straight-line motion.
Take a particle that completes one full lap of a circular track and returns to its starting point.
Here average speed is nonzero but the magnitude of average velocity is zero, so the two are not equal.
steps.why_this_step: A single counterexample is enough to disprove an always-true claim.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the statement is true because it holds for straight-line motion in one direction, without checking motion that changes direction or returns to the start.

question.text: A body is projected vertically upward from the ground with a launch speed u. It crosses an elevation of 80 m at two different instants, such that the time gap between these two occurrences is 6 s. Calculate the initial speed u. (Take g = 10 m/s²)
conditions: time difference between identical heights = 6 s

figure.description: A sketch illustrating the vertical path of an object thrown upwards from the ground with initial speed u, showing it at a height of 80 m during ascent and descent, with an upward positive sign convention.

solution.approach: Write the height equation as a quadratic in time, use the sum and product of its two roots, and apply the given 6 s gap between them.

steps.text: Write the height reached at time t, taking upward as positive from the ground.
Set the height to 80 m; this gives a quadratic whose two roots t₁ and t₂ are the two times the ball is at that height.
From the quadratic, write the sum and product of the roots in terms of u.
Use (t₂ − t₁)² = (t₁+t₂)² − 4t₁t₂ with the given 6 s gap to solve for u.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the 6 s gap as the single time to reach the height, and solving 80 = 6u − 5(6)² for u, giving about 43.3 m/s.

question.text: An object travels along a straight path at a constant speed v for a duration t₀, after which it continues at 2v for an equal time interval t₀. In the final portion of its motion, it moves at 3v for a duration T. If the mean velocity over the entire journey is equal to 2.5 v, determine the value of T expressed using t₀.
conditions: constant velocity in each phase of motion
speed is v for duration t₀
speed is 2v for subsequent duration t₀

solution.approach: Write the total displacement as the sum of the three constant-velocity legs, divide by the total time to set it equal to the given average velocity, and solve for T.

steps.text: Write the displacement covered in each of the three legs of the journey.
steps.equation: leg 1: v t₀, leg 2: 2v t₀, leg 3: 3v T

steps.text: Add these for the total displacement and add the three times for the total time.
steps.equation: total displacement = 3v t₀ + 3vT, total time = 2t₀ + T

steps.text: Set the total displacement over the total time equal to the given average velocity of 2.5v.
Cancel v and solve the resulting linear equation for T.

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out the displacement of the first leg, v t₀, from the total when setting up the equation gives T = 6t₀.

question.text: An object is thrown straight up into the air and attains its highest point H after a duration T. Find the vertical position of this object at an arbitrary instant t (where t < T).
conditions: motion under constant gravitational acceleration g
reaches maximum height H at time T

solution.approach: Write the height at time t using the launch speed and g, express the launch speed with H and T, then rewrite the height using H and T alone.

steps.text: Since the particle reaches maximum height H at time T, the launch speed is u = gT. Write the height at any time t.
Express H using u and g, then substitute u = gT.
Take option d and expand it to check whether it equals y(t).
steps.equation: H − ½g(T − t)² = ½gT² − ½g(T² − 2Tt + t²) = gTt − ½gt²

steps.text: This matches y(t) exactly, so option d is the correct expression for the height at time t.

common_mistakes.text: Dropping the factor of ½ while expanding H − ½g(T − t)², giving H − g(T − t)², which is a different, smaller expression.
Writing only the offset-from-the-top term ½g(T − t)² and forgetting to subtract it from H, which gives the distance fallen from the top, not the height above the ground.

question.text:
Assertion: For the velocity versus time plot shown, the average velocity throughout the duration from 0 to t₀ relies purely on v₀ and does not depend on t₀.
Reason: Throughout this specified time span, the mean velocity has a value of v₀/2.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: motion from time t = 0 to t = t₀
velocity starts from zero at t = 0, increases linearly to peak v₀, and decreases linearly back to zero at t = t₀

figure.description: A velocity-time graph with velocity v on the vertical axis and time t on the horizontal axis. Starting from the origin O, the line increases linearly to a maximum velocity v₀ and then decreases linearly back to zero at time t₀, forming a single triangle between the line and the time axis.

solution.approach: The area of the triangular v-t graph, and so the average velocity, depends only on the base and height, not on where the peak sits along the base.

steps.text: The distance travelled from 0 to t₀ is the area of the triangle formed by the v-t graph.
steps.equation: Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × t₀ × v₀

steps.text: This area formula holds no matter where along the base the peak occurs, so it depends only on t₀ and v₀, and t₀ cancels when finding average velocity.
steps.equation: Average velocity = Area / t₀ = (½ t₀ v₀) / t₀ = v₀/2

steps.text: The average velocity is v₀/2, which depends only on v₀ and not on t₀, so both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason directly gives the result stated in the Assertion.
steps.equation: Assertion true, Reason true, Reason explains Assertion

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the average velocity formula v₀/2 only works when the peak is at the midpoint of t₀, and marking the Reason false for a graph where the peak is off-centre.

question.text: Along a straight horizontal line parallel to the positive x-axis, two bodies labeled 1 and 2 are in motion. Initially, body 1 is positioned 40 m to the left of body 2. At the initial instant, body 1 moves with a speed of 12 m/s and experiences a constant acceleration of 4 m/s², while body 2 moves with a speed of 4 m/s and has a constant acceleration of 12 m/s², with all velocities and accelerations oriented toward the positive x-direction. Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the instant at which the separation between the two bodies reaches its smallest value.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the smallest separation between the two bodies.

conditions: initial velocity of particle 1 is 12 m/s in +x direction
constant acceleration of particle 1 is 4 m/s² in +x direction
initial velocity of particle 2 is 4 m/s in +x direction
constant acceleration of particle 2 is 12 m/s² in +x direction

figure.description: A horizontal straight line representing the x-axis points to the right as the positive direction. Body 1 is located to the left with an initial velocity vector of 12 m/s and an acceleration vector of 4 m/s² directed to the right. Body 2 is located 40 m to the right of body 1, having an initial velocity vector of 4 m/s and an acceleration vector of 12 m/s² pointing to the right.

solution.approach: Write the separation between the two particles as a function of time and minimize it using calculus.

steps.text: Take particle 1 to start at x = 0 and particle 2 at x = 40 m, and write each position using its own velocity and acceleration.
The separation is particle 2's position minus particle 1's position.
The separation is minimum when its rate of change with time is zero.
Substitute t = 1 s into the separation equation to get the minimum distance.

common_mistakes.text: Writing the position as vt + at² instead of vt + ½at² gives a minimum at t = 0.5 s and a wrong minimum distance of 38 m.
Taking the initial separation of 40 m as the minimum distance, without checking that the gap first closes and then opens again.

question.text: A particle has velocity v = (2î) m/s at the start, and its acceleration varies with time t as a = (4tî + t²ĵ) m/s². Can the kinematic relation v = u + at be applied directly to find its velocity at a later time?

solution.approach: The formula v = u + at holds only for constant acceleration; since the acceleration here depends on time, velocity must be found by integrating it over time instead.

steps.text: The equation v = u + at is derived by integrating a constant acceleration over time, dv = a dt with a fixed.
steps.equation: v = u + at, valid only when a does not change with time

steps.text: Here the acceleration is a(t) = 4tî + t²ĵ, which changes with time, so v = u + at cannot be applied directly.
steps.equation: a(t) depends on t, so v(t) = u + ∫a(t) dt, not u + a(t)·t

steps.text: As a check, at t = 1 s the wrong formula gives v = u + a(1)×1 = (2,0) + (4,1) = (6,1) m/s, while correctly integrating gives v(1) = (4, 1/3) m/s, a different result.
steps.why_this_step: The mismatch confirms that plugging the instantaneous acceleration into v = u + at gives an incorrect velocity when acceleration is not constant.

final_answer.value: No. The equation v = u + at applies only for constant acceleration; here the acceleration depends on time, so velocity must be obtained by integrating a(t) with respect to time.

common_mistakes.text: Substituting the acceleration at an instant into v = u + at as if it were constant gives v = (6, 1) m/s at t = 1 s instead of the correct (4, 1/3) m/s.

question.text: A particle travels along a straight path with a velocity that varies with time as depicted in the graph. Draw the corresponding position-time (s−t) graph of the motion, given that the particle is at s = 0 when t = 0.
conditions: velocity increases linearly from 0 to 10 m/s between t = 0 and t = 2 s
velocity remains constant at 10 m/s between t = 2 s and t = 4 s
velocity increases linearly from 10 m/s to 20 m/s between t = 4 s and t = 6 s
velocity decreases linearly from 20 m/s to 0 m/s between t = 6 s and t = 8 s

figure.description: A velocity-time (v−t) graph with v (in m/s) on the vertical axis and t (in s) on the horizontal axis. The graph consists of four straight-line segments connecting the points: O(0, 0) to A(2, 10), A(2, 10) to B(4, 10), B(4, 10) to C(6, 20), and C(6, 20) to D(8, 0).

solution.approach: Find the displacement at each corner time from the area under the v-t graph, then describe the curvature of the s-t graph in each interval.

steps.text: Find the displacement at t = 2, 4, 6, 8 s by adding the area under each straight segment of the v-t graph.
From 0 to 2 s the velocity rises from 0 to 10 m/s, so the s-t curve is concave up, steepening. From 2 to 4 s the velocity is constant at 10 m/s, so the s-t curve is a straight line.
steps.equation: 0–2 s: concave up, 2–4 s: straight line of slope 10

steps.text: From 4 to 6 s the velocity rises again from 10 to 20 m/s, so the s-t curve is concave up, steepening further. From 6 to 8 s the velocity falls from 20 to 0, so the s-t curve is concave down, flattening to a horizontal tangent at t = 8 s.
steps.equation: 4–6 s: concave up, 6–8 s: concave down, tangent horizontal at t = 8 s

final_answer.value: The s-t graph passes through (0,0), (2,10), (4,30), (6,60), (8,80) m in metres and seconds. It is concave up on 0–2 s and 4–6 s, a straight line on 2–4 s, and concave down on 6–8 s, flattening to a horizontal tangent at the maximum displacement of 80 m at t = 8 s.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing straight lines between the four displacement values ignores that the velocity is changing within each interval, which curves the s-t graph rather than making it a series of straight segments.

question.text: A person starting from point A on one bank of a river intends to reach point B located on the opposing bank downstream. The straight line joining A to B is inclined at an angle of 45° to the line perpendicular to the banks. The water moves at a uniform speed u parallel to the banks.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the lowest possible speed of the person relative to the water that allows them to reach point B.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the heading angle θ (measured upstream from the line perpendicular to the river bank) at which the person must swim.

conditions: river flows horizontally at constant speed u
line AB is inclined at 45° downstream relative to the line perpendicular to the banks
motion relative to water is uniform
man travels directly along the straight path AB

figure.description: A river of uniform width flows horizontally to the right with velocity u. Point A is situated on the bottom bank, and point B is located on the top bank downstream. A perpendicular dashed line across the river from A makes an angle of 45° with the straight line AB connecting A and B.

solution.approach: The resultant velocity must lie along AB, so the swimmer's velocity relative to water is least when perpendicular to AB; find it by resolving flow along and perpendicular to AB.

steps.text: Take x along the flow (downstream) and y straight across the river. Since AB makes 45° with the straight-across direction, the flow direction makes 45° with AB.
steps.equation: angle between the flow velocity u and the line AB = 45°

steps.text: The man's resultant velocity relative to the ground must lie along AB. His velocity relative to water, v, satisfies v = v_resultant − u, so v is the vector from the tip of u to some point on the line AB.
Among all points on the line AB, the shortest vector from the tip of u to the line is the perpendicular distance from that point to the line, so the minimum |v| occurs when v is perpendicular to AB.
steps.why_this_step: The perpendicular distance from a point to a line through the origin at angle θ to the point's direction is (distance of point from origin) × sin θ.

final_answer.value: Minimum speed relative to water = u/√2, swum in the direction perpendicular to AB (tilted upstream), which makes 45° with the line perpendicular to the banks, tilted upstream.

common_mistakes.text: Swimming straight across (perpendicular to the bank) at speed u instead of perpendicular to AB gives a larger required speed and does not minimize |v|, since it ignores that AB is tilted from straight across.

question.text: A body is thrown vertically upward with an initial speed of 40 m/s. Taking the upward direction as positive and assuming g = 10 m/s², draw the acceleration-time (a-t), velocity-time (v-t), and displacement-time (s-t) curves representing its entire motion until it returns to the launch level.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Velocity-time (v-t) graph

parts.label: c

solution.approach: Use the equations of motion under constant gravity with upward positive to find the times, then plot each quantity against time.

Find the maximum height reached.
Find the total time of flight back to the starting point.
Describe the a-t graph: acceleration stays constant throughout, since gravity does not change.

steps.text: Describe the s-t graph using s = ut + ½at², which is symmetric about the highest point.

question.text: The length of the second hand of a clock is 2.0 cm. Determine the average speed along with the magnitude of the average velocity of its tip over a time interval of 15 s.
conditions: length of second hand r = 2.0 cm
second hand completes one full rotation in 60 s with constant angular speed

solution.approach: The tip moves at constant speed around a circle of radius 2.0 cm; find the quarter-turn distance for speed and the chord length for velocity.

steps.text: The second hand's tip moves on a circle of radius 2.0 cm and completes one full turn in 60 s.
In 15 s the tip sweeps a quarter turn, so the distance travelled is a quarter of the circumference.
Average speed is this distance divided by the time.
The displacement is the straight chord between the start point and the point a quarter turn later, which are 90° apart on the circle.
Average velocity magnitude is this displacement divided by the time.
steps.why_this_step: Displacement is the straight-line chord, which is shorter than the curved arc distance.

final_answer.value: average speed ≈ 0.21 cm/s (π/15 cm/s); average velocity magnitude ≈ 0.19 cm/s (2√2/15 cm/s)

common_mistakes.text: Using the full circumference 4π cm for the 15 s interval instead of the quarter-turn distance π cm, giving an average speed of about 0.84 cm/s.
Treating the arc distance and the chord displacement as the same length, giving 0.21 cm/s for both average speed and average velocity.

question.text: Two bodies travel along the same linear path. At time t = 0, both pass through a fixed point A simultaneously. Determine the distance covered by the bodies from point A up to the moment when one catches up with the other.

both bodies pass point A at time t = 0
first body has initial speed 2u and constant acceleration a
second body has initial speed u and constant acceleration 2a

solution.approach: Write the position of each object from point A as a function of time and set them equal at the overtaking instant.

steps.text: Write the position of the first object (initial velocity 2u, acceleration a) from A.
Write the position of the second object (initial velocity u, acceleration 2a) from A.
Set the positions equal at the overtaking time and solve for t.
steps.equation: 2ut + ½at² = ut + at² → ut = ½at² → t = 2u/a

steps.text: Substitute t = 2u/a into the first object's position to get the distance moved.

question.text: The trajectory of an object follows the path y = x²/2, with its horizontal position changing over time according to x = t²/2 (where x and y are given in metres and t is given in seconds). Find the velocity vector of this object at the instant t = 2 s (in m s⁻¹).

Write y in terms of t by substituting x = t²/2 into y = x²/2.
Differentiate y with respect to t to get the y-component of velocity.
Evaluate both components at t = 2 s.
Write the velocity vector at t = 2 s.

question.text: An object moves along the positive x-axis having an initial speed of 2.5 m/s and experiences a constant acceleration of 0.50 m/s².

parts.label: b

uniform acceleration = 0.50 m/s² in positive x-direction

steps.text: Find the distance in the first 2 seconds using s = ut + ½at².

Find the distance covered in reaching 7.5 m/s using v² = u² + 2as.
Collecting the three results gives the full answer.

question.text: From the top of a 60 m tall structure, an object is thrown vertically upward with an initial speed of 20 m/s. Considering the entire duration of motion until it hits the ground, determine: (Use g = 10 m/s²)

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the average speed of the object

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the average velocity of the object

conditions: interval ends when the particle hits the ground

solution.approach: Find the time of flight from launch to landing below the tower, then use the total path length for average speed and the net displacement for average velocity.

steps.text: Take upward as positive from the roof. The particle lands 60 m below the roof, so its displacement is −60 m.
Solve this quadratic for the time of flight.
Find the extra height it rises above the roof before falling back.
Add the rise above the roof and the fall from that highest point to the ground for the total path length.
Divide the total distance by the time of flight for average speed, and the net displacement by the same time for average velocity.
steps.equation: average speed = 100/6 ≈ 16.7 ms⁻¹, average velocity = −60/6 = −10 ms⁻¹ (10 ms⁻¹ downward)

final_answer.value: (a) average speed = 100/6 ≈ 16.7 ms⁻¹, (b) average velocity = 10 ms⁻¹, directed downward

question.text:
Assertion: When two objects with different masses m₁ and m₂ are released from an identical elevation under identical drag forces from air, they hit the ground simultaneously.
Reason: The downward acceleration during fall differs between masses m₁ and m₂ when they experience identical opposing air forces.

options.1: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.2: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
options.4: Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

conditions: released from rest at the same height
equal air resistance on both objects
acceleration due to gravity is constant

solution.approach: Apply Newton's second law to each body under gravity and the same air resistance, and compare the resulting accelerations.

steps.text: Write the net force equation for each body falling under gravity with the same air resistance R.
steps.equation: m₁g − R = m₁a₁, m₂g − R = m₂a₂

steps.text: Solve each equation for the acceleration.
steps.equation: a₁ = g − R/m₁, a₂ = g − R/m₂

steps.text: Compare the two accelerations for unequal masses.
steps.equation: since m₁ ≠ m₂, R/m₁ ≠ R/m₂, so a₁ ≠ a₂

steps.text: Bodies dropped from the same height with different accelerations reach the ground at different times, so the Assertion is false, while the Reason correctly states that the accelerations differ.

final_answer.value: Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

question.text: A rock is projected straight up into the air. As it passes through half of its highest elevation, it travels at a speed of 10 ms⁻¹. Determine the peak elevation achieved by the rock. (Take g = 10 ms⁻²)
conditions: speed at half of maximum height is 10 ms⁻¹
speed at maximum height is 0 ms⁻¹

solution.approach: Use the equation of motion between the launch point and the halfway point, with speed zero at maximum height, to eliminate the initial speed and find the maximum height.

steps.text: Let u be the launch speed and H the maximum height. Since the speed is zero at the top, u² = 2gH.
Apply v² = u² − 2g(H/2) at the halfway point, where the speed is 10 ms⁻¹.
Substitute u² = 2gH into this equation.
Solve for H using g = 10 ms⁻².

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the speed falls in proportion to height, so the launch speed is twice 10 ms⁻¹, gives H = 20²/(2×10) = 20 m.

Add the magnitudes of the six areas for the total distance travelled, then divide by the total time for the average speed.

question.text: When a person travels horizontally at 3 km/h, raindrops seem to descend straight vertically downwards. If the person speeds up to 6 km/h in the same direction, the falling rain appears to strike at an angle of 45° relative to the vertical. Determine the true speed of the rain.

question.text: A rock is released from rest at the summit of a tall structure. Exactly 1 s later, another rock is projected straight downwards from the identical spot at a speed of 20 ms⁻¹. Determine how far the second rock falls before it catches up with the first rock. (Take g = 10 ms⁻²)
conditions: initial downward velocity of second stone is 20 ms⁻¹

solution.approach: Write the distance fallen by each stone measured from the same start of timing, and set them equal at the overtaking instant.

steps.text: Let t be the time measured from when the first stone is dropped. Write the distance fallen by the first stone.
The second stone starts 1 s later with initial speed 20 m/s downward. Write its distance fallen for t ≥ 1 s.
Set the two distances equal, since the second stone overtakes the first at the same position.
Expand and solve for t.
Substitute t = 1.5 s into the first stone's distance to get the overtaking distance.

question.text: An object is projected straight upward into the air. Which one of the following physical properties does not change during its flight: speed, kinetic energy, velocity, or acceleration?

solution.approach: Check each quantity through the flight: speed and kinetic energy fall to zero and rise again, velocity keeps changing, only the acceleration stays the same.

steps.text: Speed decreases from launch to the highest point, where it becomes zero, then increases again on the way down, so speed does not stay constant.
Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so it also falls to zero at the top and rises again, so it does not stay constant either.
Velocity is a vector; its magnitude changes throughout the flight and its direction reverses at the top, so velocity does not stay constant.

Acceleration is g downward at every instant of the flight, including at the highest point, since gravity acts the whole time without change, so the acceleration is the one quantity that remains constant.
steps.why_this_step: Acceleration depends on the constant force of gravity, not on the changing velocity.

common_mistakes.text: Picking speed as constant by only thinking about the upward journey and forgetting that speed falls to zero at the top and rises again on the way down.
