Picking velocity as constant, confusing it with the constant acceleration; velocity itself keeps changing in both magnitude and direction.

question.text: A lift with an interior height of 2.7 m begins moving upward from rest with a steady acceleration of 1.2 m/s². Exactly 2 s after it begins its motion, a loose bolt becomes detached from its roof. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the duration of time until the bolt strikes the floor of the lift.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the total displacement and the total distance covered by the bolt relative to the ground.

conditions: bolt detaches at t = 2 s after elevator starts moving
bolt undergoes free fall under gravity after detachment

solution.approach: In the elevator's frame the bolt falls the floor-to-ceiling gap from rest under acceleration g + a; convert the result to the ground frame for displacement and distance.

steps.text: At the instant of release, the bolt shares the elevator's velocity, so its velocity relative to the elevator is zero. In the elevator's frame the bolt falls under gravity plus the elevator's own upward acceleration.
steps.equation: relative acceleration = g + a = 9.8 + 1.2 = 11.0 m/s², relative initial velocity = 0

steps.text: The bolt must fall the floor-to-ceiling distance of 2.7 m relative to the car. Use d = ½(g+a)τ² to find the time.
For part (b), find the elevator's velocity at the moment of release: it started from rest 2 s earlier with acceleration 1.2 m/s².
In the ground frame the bolt's velocity is 2.4 m/s upward at release and then decelerates under g alone; find its net displacement over τ ≈ 0.70 s using y = v_release·τ − ½gτ².
steps.why_this_step: The negative value means the bolt ends up about 0.72 m below its release point with respect to the earth.

steps.text: The bolt rises before falling back, since it stops rising at τ_top = v_release/g ≈ 0.245 s, reaching a height of about 0.29 m above the release point. The total distance travelled is this rise plus the fall back down to the final position.

final_answer.value: (a) about 0.70 s, (b) net displacement about 0.72 m downward (with respect to the earth) and distance travelled about 1.31 m

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the elevator floor moves at the release velocity 2.4 m/s with no further acceleration, instead of accelerating at 1.2 m/s², gives a landing time of about 0.74 s instead of the correct 0.70 s.

question.text: An insect is situated at one vertex of a cube-shaped enclosure having side length a. If it travels along the inner surfaces at a steady speed u, determine the shortest time needed for it to arrive at the diagonally opposite corner.
conditions: cubical room with edge length a
motion restricted to the inner surfaces of the cube
minimum travel time along the shortest surface path

solution.approach: Unfold two adjacent faces of the cube into a flat rectangle and find the straight-line distance across it, since the ant is restricted to the surface.

steps.text: The shortest surface path between opposite corners of a cube is found by unfolding two adjacent faces into one flat rectangle.
In the unfolded rectangle, the path from corner to corner runs across a rectangle of length 2a and width a.
Find the length of the straight diagonal of this rectangle, which is the shortest surface path.
Divide by the ant's constant speed to get the minimum time.

common_mistakes.text: Using the straight-line distance through the inside of the cube (the space diagonal √3 a) instead of the shortest path along the surface, which the ant is restricted to.
Treating the shortest route as a path along three edges of the cube, giving a distance of 3a instead of the shorter diagonal path across two unfolded faces.

question.text: A rocket is launched straight upwards from ground level with an effective upward acceleration of 10 m/s². Its propellant burns out completely after 1 min, after which the rocket keeps ascending freely under gravity. Take g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the maximum altitude reached by the rocket above the ground.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Calculate the time elapsed from the moment the fuel burns out until it reaches this maximum altitude.

conditions: starts from rest at ground level
constant net upward acceleration = 10 m/s² during powered phase
free flight under gravity after engine cutoff

solution.approach: Find the speed and height reached at the end of the 1 minute of powered flight, then treat the rest of the rise as free motion decelerating under gravity alone.

steps.text: During the powered phase, the rocket starts from rest and accelerates at 10 m/s² for 60 s. Find the speed and height reached at burnout.
After the fuel finishes, only gravity acts, so the rocket decelerates at g = 10 m/s² until its speed falls to zero.
Find the extra height gained while decelerating from 600 ms⁻¹ to rest.
Add the two heights for the maximum height above the ground.

final_answer.value: (a) maximum height = 36000 m (36 km), (b) time from fuel finish to maximum height = 60 s

common_mistakes.text: Stopping the calculation at burnout and treating 18000 m, the height at fuel finish, as the maximum height, missing that the rocket keeps rising after the fuel runs out.

question.text: At initial moment t = 0, three bodies A, B, and C occupy the corners of an equilateral triangle with side length d. Throughout the motion, each body maintains an unchanging speed v. The direction of motion of A is continuously oriented toward B, B always moves toward C, and C continuously aims at A. Determine the duration after which all three bodies will converge together.
conditions: initial shape is an equilateral triangle of side d
constant speed v for all three bodies
body A always directs its velocity towards B
body B always directs its velocity towards C
body C always directs its velocity towards A

figure.description: An equilateral triangle ABC has vertices A, B, and C separated by side length d. Velocity vectors of constant magnitude v are directed along AB for particle A, along BC for particle B, and along CA for particle C. The interior angle at each corner is 60°.

solution.approach: By symmetry the triangle stays equilateral while shrinking, so find the constant rate at which side AB shortens using the components of the two particles' velocities along AB.

steps.text: By the symmetry of the three particles' motion, the triangle they form stays equilateral at every instant while it shrinks and rotates about the centroid.
steps.equation: the interior angle at every vertex stays 60° throughout the motion

steps.text: Particle A moves along AB with speed v, so its full velocity v is directed along AB, reducing the separation AB at rate v.
steps.equation: component of A's velocity along AB = v

steps.text: Particle B moves along BC with speed v. Since the angle between BA and BC is 60°, B's velocity has a component along BA (toward A) equal to v cos 60°.
steps.equation: component of B's velocity toward A = v cos 60° = v/2

steps.text: The rate at which the distance AB shortens is the sum of these two components, and this rate stays constant because the 60° angle never changes.
Since AB shortens at the constant rate 3v/2 starting from side d, the particles meet when AB reaches zero.
steps.why_this_step: A quantity decreasing at a constant rate from d to 0 takes time equal to the initial value divided by the rate.

final_answer.value: The three particles meet at time t = 2d/(3v).

common_mistakes.text: Using only the direct closing speed v (ignoring the second particle's component toward the first) gives a meeting time of d/v instead of the correct 2d/(3v).

question.text: A rock is released from rest at the summit of a vertical structure. At the moment it descends past a level 5 m beneath the summit, a second rock is released from rest at a location 25 m beneath the summit. If both objects hit the ground at the same instant, calculate the total height of the structure. (Take g = 10 m/s²).
conditions: first stone dropped from top of tower
second stone released when first stone has fallen 5 m
second stone released from a height 25 m below the top
both stones reach the ground at the same time
motion purely under uniform vertical gravity

solution.approach: Find the head-start time of the first stone, write each stone's arrival time at the bottom in terms of the tower height, and set them equal.

steps.text: The first stone falls 5 m before the second stone is released. Find this time from the free-fall equation.

Let H be the tower height. The first stone reaches the bottom at time T given by falling the full height H, and the second stone (released 1 s later, from 25 m below the top) reaches the bottom after falling (H − 25) m.
Both stones reach the bottom at the same instant, so the second stone's fall time plus its 1 s delay equals the first stone's total fall time.
Solve this equation for H.
steps.why_this_step: Checking: T = √(45/5) = 3 s, and t₂ = √(20/5) = 2 s, so the second stone arrives at 1 + 2 = 3 s, matching T.

common_mistakes.text: Using the linear relation t = d/g instead of d = ½gt² for the first stone's 5 m fall gives t₁ = 0.5 s instead of the correct 1 s.

question.text: Two automobiles, A and B, start from rest and move along a straight track with constant accelerations a₁ and a₂ respectively to cover the same distance. Car A completes the race in a time interval t shorter than car B, and crosses the endpoint with a speed exceeding that of car B by v. Show that the relationship between these quantities is given by v = √(a₁a₂) t.
conditions: constant acceleration a₁ for car A
constant acceleration a₂ for car B
both cars cover the same total distance

solution.approach: Write the time each car takes to reach the same finish distance from rest, then form the given time difference and speed difference and divide one by the other.

steps.text: Let d be the distance to the finish line. Since both cars start from rest with constant acceleration, write each car's time to cover d.
steps.equation: d = ½a₁t_A² ⟹ t_A = √(2d/a₁), d = ½a₂t_B² ⟹ t_B = √(2d/a₂)

steps.text: Car A takes a time t less than car B, so form t_B minus t_A.
Car A's finishing speed exceeds car B's by v, so form v_A minus v_B using v = at for each car.
Divide the speed difference by the time difference; the common factor √(2d)(√a₁ − √a₂) cancels.
steps.why_this_step: Both v and t were written in terms of the same distance d, so d cancels out of the ratio and only a₁, a₂, t remain.

final_answer.value: v = √(a₁a₂) t, proved by expressing t = t_B − t_A and v = v_A − v_B in terms of the common finishing distance d and dividing.

common_mistakes.text: Using v = a₁t or v = a₂t with one shared t, instead of each car's own finish time, ignores the actual difference and gives no relation to the t and v of the problem.

question.text: An object initially at rest speeds up with a steady acceleration of 4 m/s² throughout the first 4 s. Following this, it slows down at a constant rate over the subsequent 8 s until it halts completely. For the entire duration of this journey, determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: average acceleration

parts.label: b
parts.asks: average speed

parts.label: c
parts.asks: average velocity

conditions: constant acceleration of 4 m/s² for 4 s
uniform deceleration for the next 8 s

solution.approach: Find the peak speed reached after the acceleration phase, then use it to find the distance covered in each phase, and combine everything over the full 12 seconds.

steps.text: The particle starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 4 s, reaching a peak speed.
It then slows uniformly from 16 ms⁻¹ to rest over the next 8 s.
Find the distance covered in each of the two phases.
Add the two distances and the two times for the total distance and total time.
steps.equation: total distance = 32 + 64 = 96 m, total time = 4 + 8 = 12 s

steps.text: The particle starts and ends at rest, so its total change in velocity over the whole 12 s is zero, giving zero average acceleration; the motion never reverses direction, so the average speed and the average velocity both equal the total distance over the total time.
steps.equation: average acceleration = (0 − 0)/12 = 0, average speed = average velocity = 96/12 = 8 ms⁻¹

final_answer.value: (a) average acceleration = 0, (b) average speed = 8 ms⁻¹, (c) average velocity = 8 ms⁻¹

common_mistakes.text: Averaging the two acceleration magnitudes, 4 m/s² and 2 m/s², directly without weighting by time or sign, gives 3 m/s² for the average acceleration instead of 0.

question.text: An object moves along a straight path such that it maintains a constant speed v₁ for the initial half of its total travel duration, and a constant speed v₂ for the final half of the duration. Determine the average speed of the object throughout the entire trip.
conditions: speed during first half of total time is v₁
speed during second half of total time is v₂

figure.description: A line segment from point A to point B split at a point C into two sections: section AC corresponds to duration t, speed v₁, and distance d₁; section CB corresponds to duration t, speed v₂, and distance d₂.

solution.approach: When the two speeds each last for equal time, the average speed is the arithmetic mean, found from total distance over total time.

steps.text: Let each half of the total time be t, so the total time is 2t.
Find the distance covered in each half from distance = speed multiplied by time.
Average speed is total distance over total time.
Cancel t and simplify.

common_mistakes.text: Using the harmonic mean 2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂), which applies only when the two parts are equal in distance, not equal in time.

question.text: A vehicle travels horizontally along a direct path at a steady speed of 30 ms⁻¹. An object is launched straight up from this vehicle so that it lands back at its exact launching spot after the vehicle has traveled a distance of 80 m. What is the required launch speed with respect to the vehicle? (Use g = 10 ms⁻²)
conditions: cart moves horizontally at constant speed 30 ms⁻¹
particle projected vertically upwards relative to the cart
particle lands back at its launch point on the cart after the cart travels 80 m

solution.approach: Find the time of flight from the cart's speed and distance moved, then use it as the projectile's up-and-down time to find launch speed relative to the cart.

steps.text: The cart moves at constant speed 30 ms⁻¹ and covers 80 m while the projectile is in the air. Find the time of flight.
Relative to the cart, the projectile only moves vertically: straight up and back down to the same point on the cart. This is the usual vertical time of flight.
Solve for the vertical launch speed relative to the cart.

question.text: An individual takes 90 s to climb up a stationary 15 m escalator. If the individual remains motionless on the same escalator while it operates, they reach the top in 60 s.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the duration needed for the individual to walk upwards while the escalator is running.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Does this calculated time rely on the length of the escalator?

conditions: time taken walking on stationary escalator = 90 s
time taken standing on moving escalator = 60 s
walking speed relative to escalator is constant
escalator moves at a constant speed

solution.approach: Find the walking speed and the escalator speed separately, in escalator lengths per second, then add them for the combined speed.

steps.text: Write the walking speed as the escalator length divided by the walking time, and the escalator speed as the length divided by the moving time.
Add the two speeds, since walking on the moving escalator combines both motions.
Divide the escalator length by the combined speed to get the time; notice that the length appears in both the numerator and the denominator.
steps.why_this_step: Since t = L ÷ (L/90 + L/60), the length L cancels, so the time does not depend on how long the escalator is.

final_answer.value: 36 s; no, the answer does not depend on the escalator length, since the length cancels out of the calculation.

common_mistakes.text: Averaging the two given times as (90 + 60)/2 gives 75 s, which is not how the walking and escalator speeds combine.

question.text: A particle travels along a straight path. At a particular moment, its speed is 10 m/s, and its velocity drops at a rate of 3 m/s per metre of displacement. Calculate the acceleration of the object at that instant.
conditions: velocity decreases at 3 m/s per metre of displacement
velocity is 10 m/s at the specified instant

solution.approach: Acceleration equals velocity times the rate of change of velocity with displacement, a = v(dv/ds).

steps.text: Write acceleration using the chain rule for motion described by velocity as a function of displacement.
The velocity decreases at 3 m/s for every metre of displacement, so dv/ds is negative.
Substitute v = 10 m/s and dv/ds = −3 (m/s)/m into a = v(dv/ds) to get the acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: a = v dv/ds is the standard way to find acceleration when velocity is given as a function of position, not time.

common_mistakes.text: Dropping the negative sign on the rate of decrease and writing a = 10 × 3 = 30 m/s².
Writing a = dv/ds = −3 m/s² directly, leaving out the factor of v from the chain rule.

question.text: An elevator is moving downwards while speeding up. Determine the direction of its velocity and the direction of its acceleration during this motion.

solution.approach: A lift descending means its velocity points downward; its speed increasing while descending means the acceleration must point in the same direction as the velocity.

steps.text: The lift is descending, so its velocity is directed downward.
The speed is increasing while the lift moves downward, so the acceleration must act in the same sense as the velocity to speed the lift up rather than slow it down.
steps.why_this_step: When acceleration points in the same direction as velocity, speed increases; when it points opposite, speed decreases.

final_answer.value: Both the velocity and the acceleration of the lift are directed downward.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming a descending object must always have an upward (retarding) acceleration confuses this case with a lift that is slowing down while descending, not speeding up.

question.text: A sphere is dropped from rest at the summit of a structure measuring h metre tall. If a duration of T second elapses before it hits the ground, find the location of the sphere at time T/3 second.

solution.approach: Express g in terms of h and T, find the distance fallen in the first T/3, and subtract it from h.

steps.text: Write the total height in terms of the total fall time T, using free fall from rest.
Find the distance fallen in time T/3 using this g.
Subtract the fallen distance from h to get the height above the ground.

common_mistakes.text: Correctly finding the distance fallen in T/3 as h/9, but stating that distance itself as the answer instead of subtracting it from h to get the height above the ground.

question.text: An object travels along the x-axis under uniform acceleration. Its position coordinate relative to a fixed reference point is 2 m at t = 0 and becomes 0 at t = 10 s. Given that its speed momentarily drops to zero at t = 6 s, calculate its acceleration a and its velocity v at t = 10 s.

solution.approach: Use the zero-velocity instant at t = 6 s to relate the initial velocity to the acceleration, then use the displacement at t = 10 s to solve for both.

steps.text: Write velocity as v(t) = v₀ + at and use v(6) = 0 to relate v₀ and a.
Write displacement as x(t) = 2 + v₀t + ½at² and use x(10) = 0, substituting v₀ = −6a.
Solve for a, then find v₀ and the velocity at t = 10 s.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the particle starts from rest at t = 0 instead of using the given v(6 s) = 0 condition gives a = −0.04 m/s² and v(10) = −0.4 m/s, both wrong.

question.text: A straight rigid rod of length l is placed such that its upper point B slides along a smooth vertical wall while its lower point A slides along a horizontal floor. If point A is drawn away from the wall to the left at a constant speed v, determine the downward speed of point B at the precise moment when the rod is inclined at an angle θ to the floor.
conditions: rod maintains contact with both the vertical wall and horizontal floor
lower end A moves horizontally away from the wall at constant velocity v
angle between the rod and the floor is θ

figure.description: A vertical wall and a horizontal floor form a right-angled corner. A straight rod of length l connects the two surfaces, with its upper end B touching the vertical wall and its lower end A resting on the horizontal floor. Point A is moving horizontally to the left with a constant velocity vector labelled v. The angle between the rod and the ground at point A is denoted as θ.

solution.approach: Write the constant-length constraint between the horizontal position of A and the vertical position of B, then differentiate with respect to time.

steps.text: Let x be the horizontal distance of A from the corner and y be the height of B on the wall. The rod length is fixed.
steps.equation: x² + y² = l², with x = l cos θ, y = l sin θ

steps.text: Differentiate the constraint with respect to time.
End A moves away from the wall at the given constant speed v, so dx/dt = v. Substitute x = l cos θ and y = l sin θ.
Solve for dy/dt.
steps.equation: dy/dt = −v cos θ / sin θ = −v cot θ
steps.why_this_step: The negative sign shows y is decreasing, meaning B moves downward at this rate.

final_answer.value: The velocity of end B is v cot θ, directed downward.

common_mistakes.text: Differentiating x = l cos θ and y = l sin θ but mismatching which trigonometric ratio goes with dx/dt gives v tan θ instead of the correct v cot θ.

question.text: Derive the kinematic formula for the distance traveled by an object during its t-th second of motion under constant acceleration, given by sₜ = u + at − ½ a, where u represents the initial velocity and a is the uniform acceleration.

solution.approach: Write the total distance covered up to n seconds and up to (n − 1) seconds, and subtract to get the distance in the nth second.

steps.text: Here t stands for the number of the second being counted, that is n, a whole number of seconds; write the total distance covered from the start of the motion up to n seconds using the standard distance equation.
Write the same equation for one second earlier, up to (n − 1) seconds.
The distance covered during the nth second alone is the difference of these two totals.
Expand and simplify the difference.
Write ½a(2n − 1) as an − ½a to reach the required form.
steps.why_this_step: This is exactly sₜ = u + at − ½a once t is read as the second number n.

final_answer.value: sₜ = u + at − ½a, proved by subtracting the distance covered up to (t − 1) seconds from the distance covered up to t seconds

common_mistakes.text: Substituting t directly into s = ut + ½at² and calling the result the distance in the tth second, which gives the total distance up to time t, not the distance during that one second.
Expanding (n − 1)² as n² − 1 instead of n² − 2n + 1, which drops the −2n term and changes the coefficient of a.

question.text: A watch features a second hand measuring 1 cm from the pivot to the tip. Determine the magnitude of the change in velocity of this tip over a time interval of 15 s.
conditions: length of second hand r = 1 cm
time period of rotation T = 60 s

solution.approach: Find the constant speed of the tip, the angle it sweeps in 15 s, and then the magnitude of the vector difference between the initial and final velocity.

steps.text: Find the angular speed of the seconds hand and the speed of its tip.
steps.equation: ω = 2π/60 = π/30 rad/s, v = ωr = π/30 cm/s

steps.text: Find the angle swept by the tip in 15 s.
The velocity vector keeps the same magnitude but turns through 90°, so find the magnitude of the vector difference between two perpendicular vectors of equal length.
Substitute v = π/30 cm/s to get the change in velocity.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming that because the speed (magnitude of velocity) stays constant, the velocity itself does not change, giving zero instead of accounting for the change in direction.
Using the chord formula without the factor of two, computing v sin(Δθ/2) instead of 2v sin(Δθ/2), which gives π/(30√2) cm/s.

question.text: A particle travels along a straight path such that its speed depends on its position coordinate s through the relation v = √(4 + 4s) m/s. Given that the particle is located at s = 0 at time t = 0, calculate its position coordinate at t = 2 s.

solution.approach: Separate variables in v = ds/dt = √(4 + 4s), integrate both sides from the given start, and evaluate the resulting displacement at t = 2 s.

steps.text: Write velocity as the derivative of displacement and separate the variables.
Integrate the left side from s = 0 to s and the right side from t = 0 to t.
Solve for s as a function of t.
Substitute t = 2 s to get the displacement.
steps.why_this_step: This is the closed-form displacement evaluated at the requested time.

common_mistakes.text: Treating v = √(4+4s) as v = √(4+4t) and integrating with respect to time directly, ds = √(4+4t)dt, gives a wrong displacement of about 5.6 m at t = 2 s instead of 8 m.

question.text: The velocity components of an object traveling in the xy-plane depend on time according to vₓ = 8t − 2 and v_y = 2. At time t = 2 s, the object is located at the position x = 14 and y = 4. Which of the following expressions represents the equation of its trajectory?
conditions: at t = 2 s, x = 14 and y = 4

solution.approach: Integrate both velocity components with constants of integration, fix the constants from the given point, then eliminate time between x(t) and y(t).

steps.text: Integrate the two velocity components to get position, with constants of integration.
Use the given point x = 14, y = 4 at t = 2 s to find the constants.
Write x(t) and y(t) explicitly and solve y(t) for t.
Substitute t = y/2 into x(t) to eliminate time and get the path equation.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting to solve for the constants of integration (taking C₁ = C₂ = 0) gives x = y² − y, which matches none of the printed algebraic options.

question.text: The position of an object travelling along the x-axis depends on time according to the equation X = 2t² + 4t − 6, where X is measured in metres and t in seconds. Determine the average velocity of the object from t = 0 to t = 2 s.
conditions: time interval from t = 0 to t = 2 s

solution.approach: Average velocity over an interval is the change in position divided by the change in time.

steps.text: Find the position at the two given times.
Divide the change in position by the change in time.
State the result.

common_mistakes.text: Computing the instantaneous velocity dX/dt = 4t + 4 at t = 2 s and calling it the average velocity, giving 12 m/s.
Dividing X(2) alone by 2 as if the particle started from zero, giving 10/2 = 5 m/s.

question.text: A body begins moving with an initial speed u and travels along a straight path. It covers the first half of the total distance with a constant acceleration a₁, and then covers the second half of the distance with a constant acceleration a₂. Demonstrate that its speed at the end of the journey is equal to the final speed it would attain if it traversed the entire path with a single uniform acceleration of (a₁ + a₂)/2.
conditions: first half of distance s traversed with constant acceleration a₁
second half of distance s traversed with constant acceleration a₂
compared with total distance 2s traversed with uniform acceleration (a₁ + a₂)/2

figure.description: A diagram comparing two cases of linear motion. Case 1 shows a particle starting with velocity u, traversing a displacement s under constant acceleration a₁ to reach velocity v₁, and then traversing an equal displacement s under constant acceleration a₂ to reach final velocity v₂. Case 2 shows the particle starting with velocity u, traversing the total displacement 2s under uniform acceleration (a₁ + a₂)/2, and attaining final velocity v.

solution.approach: Apply v² = u² + 2as across each half with a₁ and a₂, then compare the result with the same formula applied to the whole distance under the average acceleration.

steps.text: After the first half of distance s with acceleration a₁, the velocity v₁ satisfies this.
After the second half of distance s with acceleration a₂, starting from v₁, the velocity v₂ satisfies this.
For the whole distance 2s covered with the uniform acceleration (a₁ + a₂)/2 starting from u, the final velocity v satisfies this.
Both expressions for the squared final velocity are the same, so the final speeds are equal.
steps.why_this_step: Two non-negative quantities with equal squares must be equal.

final_answer.value: v₂ = v, so the final velocity covering the whole distance with uniform acceleration (a₁ + a₂)/2 equals the final velocity of the two-stage motion; proved as v₂² = v² = u² + 2s(a₁ + a₂).

common_mistakes.text: Applying v² = u² + 2 × (a₁ + a₂)/2 × s with distance s instead of full distance 2s gives u² + s(a₁ + a₂), which does not match v₂² and breaks the proof.

question.text: Anoop travels toward the east at a speed of 1 m/s, whereas Dhyani heads toward the west at 2 m/s. Determine the relative velocity of Anoop as observed by Dhyani.
conditions: velocity of Anoop is 1 m/s due east
velocity of Dhyani is 2 m/s due west
motion is along a straight east-west line

solution.approach: Relative velocity of one object with respect to another is the vector difference of their velocities, taken along one chosen positive direction.

steps.text: Take east as the positive direction and write both velocities.
Apply the relative velocity formula.
State the direction from the sign of the result.

common_mistakes.text: Adding the two speeds without assigning signs based on direction gives 3 m/s but with no direction, or subtracting the wrong way gives −3 m/s (west) instead of east.
Subtracting the speeds as 2 − 1 = 1 m/s ignores that the two velocities point in opposite directions.

question.text: The position of an object travelling in the xy-plane changes with time t such that its coordinates are given by x = 2t and y = 10t − 16t². Determine the equation of the path followed by this object.

solution.approach: Eliminate time between the x and y equations to get y directly in terms of x.

steps.text: Write the given x and y coordinates as functions of time.
Solve the x equation for time.
Substitute this time into the y equation and simplify.

common_mistakes.text: Substituting t = x/2 into 16t² as 16(x/2) instead of squaring the whole bracket gives y = 5x − 8x = −3x, a wrong linear equation.

question.text: Two particles begin their motion at the same instant along the x-axis. Particle 1 is initially located at x = − 10 m, moving with a speed of 4 m/s in the negative x-direction while experiencing an acceleration of 2 m/s² in the positive x-direction. Particle 2 is initially positioned at x = + 2 m, possessing an initial speed of 6 m/s in the positive x-direction and an acceleration of 2 m/s² in the negative x-direction. Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The time elapsed until the particles collide.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The position coordinate (x) at which the collision occurs.

conditions: Particle 1: initial position x = − 10 m, initial velocity = − 4 m/s, acceleration = + 2 m/s²
Particle 2: initial position x = + 2 m, initial velocity = + 6 m/s, acceleration = − 2 m/s²

figure.description: A horizontal x-axis displaying two particles. Particle 1 is at coordinate x = − 10 m with an initial velocity vector pointing leftward of magnitude 4 m/s and an acceleration vector pointing rightward of magnitude 2 m/s². Particle 2 is at coordinate x = + 2 m with an initial velocity vector pointing rightward of magnitude 6 m/s and an acceleration vector pointing leftward of magnitude 2 m/s².

solution.approach: Write the position of each particle as a function of time and solve for the time at which the two positions are equal.

steps.text: Write the position of particle 1, starting at x = −10 m with velocity −4 m/s and acceleration +2 m/s².
Write the position of particle 2, starting at x = +2 m with velocity +6 m/s and acceleration −2 m/s².
Set the two positions equal and solve the resulting quadratic for t, keeping the positive root.
Substitute t = 6 s into either position equation to get the collision point.

common_mistakes.text: Taking t = −1 s, the other root of the quadratic, as the collision time, which is not physical since time cannot be negative.
Writing particle 1's acceleration term as −t² instead of +t² by keeping the sign of its velocity for the acceleration too, which changes the quadratic and its root.

question.text: An object moves in the x-y plane starting from the location (4 m, 10 m) at t = 0. Its initial velocity vector is given by u = (4î + 8ĵ) m/s, and it experiences a constant acceleration of a = (2î − 4ĵ) m/s². Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the instant of time at which the object intersects the x-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the value of its x-coordinate at that specific moment.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: its velocity vector at that exact time.

conditions: crossing the x-axis corresponds to y = 0

figure.description: A 2D Cartesian coordinate plane showing a particle initially at point P(4 m, 10 m). Vectors drawn at point P indicate an initial velocity component of 4 m/s and an acceleration component of 2 m/s² along the positive x-axis, an initial velocity component of 8 m/s along the positive y-axis, and an acceleration component of 4 m/s² along the negative y-axis.

solution.approach: Write the y-coordinate as a function of time and find when it becomes zero, then use that time in the x-coordinate and velocity equations.

steps.text: Write the y-coordinate using the initial y-position, initial y-velocity, and y-acceleration.
Set y(t) = 0 to find when the particle crosses the x-axis, and solve the quadratic, keeping the positive root.
Write the x-coordinate using the initial x-position, initial x-velocity, and x-acceleration, and substitute t = 5 s.
Find the velocity components at t = 5 s using the given accelerations, then combine them for the speed.

common_mistakes.text: Taking t = −1 s, the other root of the quadratic, as the crossing time, which is not physical.
Writing the x-acceleration term as 2t² instead of ½(2)t² = t² gives x(5) = 4 + 20 + 50 = 74 m.

question.text: Two trains travel towards one another along a single railway track with initial speeds v₁ = 10 ms⁻¹ and v₂ = 20 ms⁻¹. Upon applying brakes, they slow down at constant rates of a₁ = 2 ms⁻² and a₂ = 1 ms⁻² respectively. Find the smallest initial gap required between the two trains so that they do not collide.
conditions: trains travel towards each other on the same straight track
initial velocities v₁ = 10 ms⁻¹ and v₂ = 20 ms⁻¹
constant retarding rates a₁ = 2 ms⁻² and a₂ = 1 ms⁻²
trains come to rest to avoid collision

solution.approach: Find how long each train keeps moving toward the other before it stops, since the faster-decelerating train stops first, then add the two stopping distances.

steps.text: Find how long each train takes to stop under its own retardation.
steps.equation: t₁ = v₁/a₁ = 10/2 = 5 s, t₂ = v₂/a₂ = 20/1 = 20 s

steps.text: Train 1 stops first, at t = 5 s. After that only train 2 is still moving toward train 1's stopped position, so the two trains keep closing until train 2 also stops at t = 20 s.
steps.why_this_step: The trains avoid collision only if the total ground each covers before stopping is less than the initial separation, so the minimum safe separation equals the sum of their stopping distances.

steps.text: Find the stopping distance of each train using v² = 2 a s.
Add the two stopping distances to get the minimum separation needed to avoid collision.

common_mistakes.text: Using the single formula (v₁+v₂)²/[2(a₁+a₂)] for the closing distance, which only applies while both trains are still moving; this gives 30²/6 = 150 m, ignoring that train 1 stops at 5 s.

question.text: A body travels in a straight line along the x-direction with its velocity governed by the equation v = (10 + 5t − t²), where v is measured in m/s and t in seconds. Given that the body is located at x = 0 when t = 0, determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The acceleration of the object at the instant t = 2 s

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The position coordinate x of the object at the instant t = 3 s

conditions: v = 10 + 5t − t² (v in m/s, t in s)

solution.approach: Differentiate the velocity once for acceleration, and integrate it from 0 to the given time for position.

steps.text: Differentiate v with respect to time to get the acceleration.
Substitute t = 2 s.
Integrate v with respect to time from 0 to 3 s to get the x-coordinate, since x = 0 at t = 0.
Evaluate the integral at t = 3 s.

common_mistakes.text: Differentiating −t² as −t instead of −2t gives an acceleration of 3 m/s² at t = 2 s instead of 1 m/s².
Multiplying the velocity at t = 3 s by 3 s instead of integrating gives 48 m instead of 43.5 m.

question.text: An elevator is ascending vertically with an upward acceleration equal to g/2. A rock is dropped from inside this lift. Immediately after it is let go, determine the acceleration of the rock.

solution.approach: Once the stone leaves the elevator, the elevator's support force is gone and only gravity acts on it.

steps.text: Before release, the stone moves with the elevator, which has acceleration g/2 upward, because the elevator floor pushes on the stone.
At the instant of release, the stone loses contact with the elevator, so the elevator's push on it becomes zero.
The only force left on the stone is its own weight, so apply Newton's second law to the stone alone.
The acceleration of the stone just after release is g, directed vertically downward.
steps.why_this_step: Once contact is lost, the stone's later motion no longer depends on how the elevator was moving.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the stone keeps the elevator's acceleration g/2 upward after release, forgetting that this required the elevator's push, which is gone.
Subtracting the elevator's acceleration from g to get g/2 downward, treating the elevator's motion as if it still acted on the released stone.

question.text:
Assertion: One object is released from rest at an elevation h while simultaneously a second object is launched straight upwards with a velocity of √(gh). The two objects will cross each other at an altitude of h/2.
Reason: Each of the two objects requires an identical duration of time to reach the vertical level h/2.

options.1: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.2: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
options.4: Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

conditions: first object dropped from rest at height h
second object projected vertically upward from ground with speed √(gh)
both objects move simultaneously under uniform gravitational acceleration g

solution.approach: Write the height above ground for both bodies as functions of time, find when they add up to h, and check that each independently reaches h/2 at that same time.

steps.text: Write the height above ground for the dropped body and the thrown-up body.
The bodies meet when their heights above ground are equal.
Substitute this time into y_B to find the meeting height.
steps.equation: y_B(√(h/g)) = h − h/2 = h/2, so the meeting height is h/2

steps.text: Find the time for the dropped body alone to fall a distance h/2, and the time for the thrown-up body alone to first rise to height h/2.
Both statements are individually true, and the equal time for the two bodies to reach h/2 is exactly why they meet there, so the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.

final_answer.value: Both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

question.text: An aircraft needs to fly from location A to a destination B, which lies 500 km away along a line 30° east of north. A constant wind blows directly northward at 20 m/s. The speed of the aircraft relative to the air is 150 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the heading direction the pilot must steer the aircraft so as to reach destination B directly.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Calculate the total duration needed for the aircraft to travel from A to B.

conditions: displacement from A to B = 500 km at 30° east of north
aircraft speed relative to air = 150 m/s
motion of aircraft relative to ground is straight along line AB

solution.approach: The wind's component across AB must be cancelled by an opposite component of the plane's airspeed; this fixes the heading, and the remaining along-path components give the ground speed.

steps.text: The wind blows due north while AB is 30° east of north, so resolve the wind across the path AB.
For the plane to travel exactly along AB, the component of its 150 m/s airspeed across AB must cancel this 10 m/s, which fixes the angle between the heading and AB.
The pilot must head 3.8° to the east of the line AB, so the heading is 30° + 3.8° = 33.8° east of north.
steps.why_this_step: Flying straight along AB with no correction would drift the plane west of B, since north (the wind direction) lies west of AB; aiming further east compensates for this.

steps.text: Find the ground speed by adding the along-AB components of the airspeed and the wind, since their across-AB components have cancelled.
Divide the 500 km distance by the ground speed to get the time, and state both results.
steps.equation: t = 500000 m / 167.0 m/s ≈ 2994 s ≈ 49.9 min; heading is 3.8° east of AB (bearing ≈ N33.8°E), time ≈ 49.9 min

final_answer.value: (a) Head the plane 3.8° east of the line AB, i.e. along bearing N33.8°E, (b) about 2994 s ≈ 49.9 minutes

common_mistakes.text: Adding the wind speed directly to the steering speed, ignoring the 30° angle between the wind and AB, gives a ground speed of 170 m/s and a shorter time of about 2941 s.
Setting sinθ = 20/150 instead of resolving the wind across AB first gives a wrong heading of about 37.7° east of north instead of 33.8°.

question.text: Water in a river of width 30 m flows downstream at a constant speed of 2 m/s. A boatman steers his boat at 5 m/s relative to the water, maintaining an angle of 37° with the direction of the river flow. Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The time taken by the boatman to cross over to the opposite bank.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The total downstream drift of the boatman upon reaching the opposite bank.

conditions: rowing velocity relative to water = 5 m/s
rowing direction = 37° to the river flow

figure.description: A river of width 30 m flows horizontally to the right with speed 2 m/s. A boat's velocity vector of magnitude 5 m/s is oriented at an angle of 37° above the horizontal downstream direction. Its components are 4 m/s along the stream (plus the 2 m/s river speed, making 6 m/s horizontally) and 3 m/s perpendicular across the stream.

solution.approach: Split the rowing velocity into a part across the river and a part along it, then add the river current to the along part.

steps.text: Resolve the rowing velocity of 5 m/s at 37° into a part across the river and a part along the river.
steps.equation: v_across = 5 sin 37° = 3 m/s, v_along = 5 cos 37° = 4 m/s

steps.text: Only the across part carries the boat over the width of 30 m, so use it to find the crossing time.
Add the river current to the along part to get the total speed along the bank, then multiply by the time to get the drift.

common_mistakes.text: Using the full 5 m/s instead of only the across component 3 m/s gives a crossing time of 6 s.
Forgetting to add the river current to the along component gives a drift of 40 m instead of 60 m.

question.text: A ball is thrown straight up into the air with an initial speed of 50 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s², determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the maximum height reached by the ball,

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the time taken to arrive at this peak altitude,

parts.label: c
parts.asks: its speed when it is at half of the peak altitude.

solution.approach: Use the standard equations for motion under constant gravity, taking upward as positive and deceleration g.

steps.text: Maximum height uses the equation relating v² to u² with v = 0 at the top.
Substitute the values to find the maximum height.
Time to reach maximum height uses v = u − gt with v = 0 at the top.
Half the maximum height is 62.5 m; use v² = u² − 2gh with this height to find the speed there.
Take the square root to get the speed at half the maximum height.
steps.why_this_step: This is the last unknown asked for, completing the three parts.

common_mistakes.text: Finding the speed at half the time to the top instead of half the height, using v = u − g(t/2) = 50 − 25 = 25 m/s, which answers a different question.
Dropping the factor of 2 in v² = u² − 2gh and using v² = u² − gh, which gives about 43.3 m/s instead of 35.36 m/s.

question.text:
The motion of a particle traveling along the x-axis is described by a velocity-time graph. At t = 0 s, the position of the particle is x = 10 m.

The velocity varies with time as follows:
• From t = 0 s to t = 2 s, velocity increases linearly from 0 m/s to 4 m/s.
• From t = 2 s to t = 8 s, velocity decreases linearly from 4 m/s to −8 m/s (crossing 0 m/s at t = 4 s).
• From t = 8 s to t = 12 s, velocity is constant at −8 m/s.
• From t = 12 s to t = 16 s, velocity increases linearly from −8 m/s to 0 m/s.

Answer the following questions based on this motion:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Draw the position-time (x versus t) graph of the particle from t = 0 s to t = 16 s.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Calculate both the average velocity and the average speed for the entire duration of the motion (from t = 0 s to t = 16 s).

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Determine the average acceleration of the particle in the time span between t = 2 s and t = 8 s.

conditions: at t = 0 s, position x = 10 m
total time interval is from t = 0 s to t = 16 s

figure.description: A velocity-time (v-t) graph where the vertical axis represents velocity v in m/s with marked values −8, 0, 4, and the horizontal axis represents time t in seconds with marked points 2, 4, 8, 12, 16. The plot starts at (0, 0), rises to (2, 4), goes down straight through (4, 0) to (8, −8), runs horizontally from (8, −8) to (12, −8), and then rises linearly to (16, 0).

solution.approach: Use the area under the velocity-time graph in each segment to build the x-coordinate step by step, then use total displacement and total distance for the averages.

steps.text: Read the graph in five straight segments: 0 to 2 s (v from 0 to 4), 2 to 4 s (v from 4 to 0), 4 to 8 s (v from 0 to −8), 8 to 12 s (v constant at −8), 12 to 16 s (v from −8 to 0).
Add each area to the running x-coordinate, starting from x = 10 m at t = 0.
Average velocity over the whole journey is the total displacement divided by the total time.
Average speed is the total distance travelled, the sum of the sizes of each segment's area, divided by the total time.
Average acceleration between t = 2 s and t = 8 s is the change in velocity divided by the change in time, read from the graph.

final_answer.value: (a) x goes 10→14→18→2→−30→−46 m at t=0,2,4,8,12,16 s; (b) average velocity = −3.5 m/s, average speed = 4.5 m/s; (c) average acceleration = −2 m/s²

common_mistakes.text: Using the total distance instead of the total displacement in the average velocity formula gives 72/16 = 4.5 m/s for both average velocity and average speed.
Dividing the velocity change by the total time 8 s instead of by the 6 s interval from t = 2 s to t = 8 s gives -1.5 m/s2 instead of -2 m/s2.

question.text: A pair of identical balls are launched straight up along the same vertical path, each with an initial speed of 40 ms⁻¹. If the second ball is released 2 s after the first, find the height above the launch point where they collide. (Take g = 10 ms⁻²)
conditions: initial speed of each ball = 40 ms⁻¹
motion along the same vertical line

solution.approach: Write the height of each ball measured from the moment each is launched, and set the two heights equal at the collision instant.

steps.text: Let t be the time measured from when the first ball is launched. Write its height.
The second ball is launched 2 s later with the same initial velocity. Write its height for t ≥ 2 s.
Set the two heights equal, since the balls collide at the same height, and solve for t.
Substitute t = 5 s into the first ball's height to get the collision height.

question.text: The position x of an object changes with time t according to the relationship √x = t + 3. Which of the following statements about its motion is correct?

options.1: velocity of the particle is inversely proportional to t
options.2: velocity of particle varies linearly with t
options.3: velocity of particle is proportional to √t
options.4: initial velocity of the particle is zero

solution.approach: Square both sides to write displacement as a function of time, then differentiate to find how velocity depends on time.

steps.text: Square both sides of the given relation to write x as a function of t.
Differentiate x with respect to t to get the velocity.
This expression is of the form v = 2t + 6, which is a straight line in t, so velocity varies linearly with time.
Check the initial velocity at t = 0 to rule out the other options.
steps.equation: v(0) = 2(0) + 6 = 6 ms⁻¹, not zero, not inversely proportional to t, and not proportional to √t

final_answer.value: velocity of particle varies linearly with t

common_mistakes.text: Differentiating t² + 6t + 9 but dropping the 6t term by mistake, leaving v = 2t, which gives v(0) = 0 instead of the correct 6 ms⁻¹.

concept_tags: velocity as a function of time

question.text: A person uses a boat to travel across a flowing river to the opposite bank. To cross in the least possible time, the journey takes 10 min, resulting in a downstream displacement of 120 m. If the crossing is instead made along the shortest possible route straight across the stream, the trip takes 12.5 min. Calculate the following quantities:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the river's width

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the boat's velocity relative to the water

parts.label: c
parts.asks: the flow speed of the current

conditions: constant boat speed relative to water
drift during minimum time crossing = 120 m

solution.approach: The minimum-time crossing uses the boat's full speed across the bank; the shortest-path crossing uses the speed left after cancelling the current, giving two equations for width and boat speed.

steps.text: In the minimum-time crossing the boat heads straight across, so the width equals boat speed times 10 min, and the current speed follows from the drift in that same time.
steps.equation: d = v_b × 10 min; v_r = 120 m / 10 min = 12 m/min

steps.text: In the shortest-path crossing the boat angles upstream so its resultant path is straight across; the effective crossing speed is reduced by the current.
Equate the two expressions for the width and solve for the boat speed.
Substitute the boat speed back to find the width, and state all three results.
steps.equation: d = 10 min × 20 m/min = 200 m; v_b = 20 m/min ≈ 0.33 m/s; v_r = 12 m/min = 0.2 m/s

final_answer.value: (a) width = 200 m, (b) boat speed relative to water = 20 m/min ≈ 0.33 m/s, (c) current speed = 12 m/min = 0.2 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Dividing the 120 m drift by the 12.5 min shortest-path time instead of the 10 min minimum-time gives a wrong current speed of 9.6 m/min instead of 12 m/min.
Writing the shortest-path speed as v_b − v_r instead of √(v_b² − v_r²) gives a wrong boat speed of 60 m/min.

question.text: An automobile travels along a straight line under uniform acceleration. It takes 6.00 s to travel the 60.0 m separation between two specific locations, reaching a speed of 15.0 m/s at the second location.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Calculate the speed of the automobile as it clears the initial point.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine the magnitude of its acceleration.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the distance behind the initial point at which the automobile was at rest.

solution.approach: Use the average of the two end speeds to find the first speed, then the definition of acceleration, then v² = u² + 2as backward to the point of rest.

steps.text: For constant acceleration, average velocity equals the average of the initial and final speeds; find it from the distance and time given.
Solve for the speed at the first point using v_avg = (v₁ + v₂)/2.
Find the acceleration from the change in speed over the 6.00 s.
Use v₁² = 2a·d to find the distance travelled from rest to the first point.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the distance divided by time, 60/6 = 10 m/s, as the speed at the first point instead of the average speed over the interval gives the wrong value for part (a).

question.text: An object travels along a straight path having a starting velocity u and experiencing a uniform acceleration a. Determine its average velocity over the duration between t = 0 and t = t seconds.
conditions: time interval from t = 0 to t = t seconds

solution.approach: Average velocity is the total displacement in the interval divided by the time, so write the displacement using the standard equation and divide by t.

steps.text: Write the displacement from 0 to time t using the standard equation of motion with constant acceleration a.
Average velocity over the interval is this displacement divided by the time taken.
Cancel t from each term to reach the simplest form.
steps.why_this_step: This also equals the mean of the initial and final velocities, (u + v)/2, since v = u + at.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the average velocity as u, the initial velocity, ignoring that the velocity keeps changing at rate a over the interval.

question.text:
Assertion: When an object begins moving from rest with an initial acceleration of zero, and its acceleration grows steadily at 2 ms⁻³, its velocity must rise at a steady rate of 1 ms⁻².
Reason: Under the stated circumstances, da/dt = 2 ms⁻³, which implies a = 2t.

options.1: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.2: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
options.4: Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

conditions: constant rate of change of acceleration da/dt = 2 ms⁻³

solution.approach: Integrate da/dt = 2 ms⁻³ starting from zero acceleration to get acceleration as a function of time, then integrate again to see how velocity actually grows.

steps.text: Integrate the given constant rate of change of acceleration, starting from zero initial acceleration, to get acceleration as a function of time.
Integrate a(t) = 2t, starting from rest, to get velocity as a function of time.

The rate at which velocity increases at any instant equals a(t) = 2t, which itself grows with time, so velocity does not increase at a constant rate; it only equals 1 ms⁻² at the single instant t = 0.5 s.
steps.equation: v(t) = t² is not linear in t, so the rate of increase of velocity is not constant

steps.text: The Assertion's claim of a constant 1 ms⁻² rate of increase is false, while the Reason correctly derives a = 2t from the given data, so the Reason is true.

final_answer.value: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Reading a = 2t at the single instant t = 0.5 s, where a = 1 ms⁻², and generalising it to a constant rate for all time.

question.text: The relationship between the speed v (in m s⁻¹) and the position s (in metres) of a body travelling along a straight track is given by v = 5√(1 + s). Choose the correct statement among the following.

options.1: The body is at rest at the start
options.2: The initial speed is 5 m s⁻¹ and the body undergoes a constant acceleration of 12.5 m s⁻²
options.3: The body continues to move at a constant speed

conditions: v is measured in m s⁻¹

solution.approach: Square the velocity-displacement equation and differentiate with respect to displacement to get the acceleration, then check the velocity at s = 0.

steps.text: Write the given relation and square both sides.
Use a = v dv/ds = d(v²/2)/ds to find the acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: This form avoids differentiating the square root directly and gives acceleration straight from v².

steps.text: Find the velocity at s = 0, the start of the motion.
The particle starts at 5 ms⁻¹ and its acceleration stays 12.5 ms⁻² for every s, so it is a constant acceleration.

final_answer.value: The motion begins with a speed of 5 m/s, and this speed keeps rising so that the rate at which it rises, the acceleration, stays fixed at 12.5 ms⁻² all along the path.

question.text: The position-time (S-t) plot of a moving object is a straight line. At time t = 0 s, its position is S = 10 m, and at time t = 5 s, its position reaches S = 0 m.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine whether this graph portrays uniform motion.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Calculate the velocity of the object.

figure.description: A plot with displacement S in meters along the vertical axis and time t in seconds along the horizontal axis shows a straight line with negative slope that starts at the point (0, 10) and crosses the horizontal axis at (5, 0).

solution.approach: A straight line on the displacement-time graph means the slope, which gives the velocity, stays constant, so the motion is uniform.

steps.text: Note the shape of the graph.
steps.equation: The S-t graph is a straight line, so its slope is the same at every point.
steps.why_this_step: A constant slope on an s-t graph means constant velocity, which is the definition of uniform motion.

steps.text: Find the slope using the two points where the line meets the axes.
State the velocity from the slope.
steps.equation: velocity = −2 m/s (magnitude 2 m/s, displacement decreasing with time)

final_answer.value: (a) uniform motion, since the s-t graph is a straight line; (b) velocity = −2 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Taking the slope as 10/5 = 2 m/s without the negative sign misses that displacement is decreasing with time.
Calling the line non-uniform because it decreases confuses a negative constant slope with a changing slope.

question.text: Water in a river flows horizontally to the right at a constant speed of 2 m/s between two parallel banks. A person starts rowing from point A on the lower bank to reach point B on the upper bank. The straight line connecting A to B makes an angle of 45° with the downstream bank. If the speed of the boat relative to the water is 4 m/s, find the angle θ with the perpendicular to the river bank at which the boat should be steered.
conditions: river flow speed v_r = 2 m/s downstream (to the right)
speed of boat relative to water |v_br| = 4 m/s
target path AB makes an angle of 45° with the bank downstream
resultant velocity of the boat is along line AB
angle θ is measured relative to the normal to the bank towards downstream

figure.description: A horizontal river with parallel banks where the current flows to the right at 2 m/s. Point A is located on the bottom bank and point B on the top bank such that the straight line AB is inclined at 45° to the horizontal river bank. A dashed line normal to the banks extends upward from point A. The boat's heading makes an angle θ to the right of this vertical dashed normal.

solution.approach: Write the resultant of the boat's velocity and the river's velocity, and require it to point along AB, which makes 45° with both the bank and the perpendicular.

steps.text: Let x be across the river along the perpendicular and y be along the bank; the boat is rowed at angle θ from the x-axis, tilted toward the flow.
Since AB makes 45° with the bank, it also makes 45° with the perpendicular, so the resultant's x and y components must be equal.
Rearrange the equation and simplify.
steps.equation: 4cos θ − 4sin θ = 2 → cos θ − sin θ = 0.5

steps.text: Solve this trigonometric equation for θ between 0° and 90°.

final_answer.value: θ ≈ 24.3° from the perpendicular to the bank, tilted toward the direction of flow

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the effect of the current and rowing straight along AB, taking θ = 45°.
Swapping the sine and cosine terms while writing the resultant components, 4sin θ − 4cos θ = 2, which gives the wrong angle θ ≈ 65.7°.

question.text: An object travels along a linear path maintaining a uniform rate of 4 m/s over a duration of 2 s, followed by traveling at 6 m/s throughout the subsequent 3 s. Determine the mean speed of the object across this entire duration.
conditions: constant speed of 4 m/s for the first 2 s
constant speed of 6 m/s for the next 3 s

solution.approach: Average speed is the total distance covered in both legs divided by the total time taken.

steps.text: Find the distance covered in the first leg.
Find the distance covered in the second leg.
Add the distances and the times.
steps.equation: total distance = 8 + 18 = 26 m, total time = 2 + 3 = 5 s

steps.text: Average speed is total distance divided by total time.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the simple average of the two speeds, (4 + 6)/2 = 5 m/s, instead of weighting each speed by the time spent at it.
Using the equal-distance average-speed formula 2v1v2/(v1 + v2) = 4.8 m/s, which only applies when the two legs cover equal distances, not equal-looking legs with different times.

question.text: A car and a truck begin moving simultaneously from rest in the same direction, with the car situated a certain distance behind the truck at the start. The truck speeds up with a uniform acceleration of 2.2 m/s², whereas the car speeds up with a steady acceleration of 3.5 m/s². By the moment the truck has covered a distance of 60 m, the car catches up with it.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: How much time is needed for the car to catch up with the truck?

parts.label: b
parts.asks: What was the initial separation between the car and the truck?

parts.label: c
parts.asks: What is the speed of each vehicle at the instant the car overtakes the truck?

conditions: both vehicles start from rest simultaneously
motion is along a straight line
distance moved by truck at overtaking = 60 m
car is initially behind the truck

solution.approach: Use s = ½at² for constant-acceleration motion from rest for both vehicles, find the time from the truck's 60 m, then find the initial gap and speeds from that time.

steps.text: Find the time for the truck to move 60 m from rest using s = ½at².
In the same time, find how far the automobile has moved from its own start.
The automobile overtakes the truck when its distance from its own start equals the truck's 60 m plus the initial gap; solve for the gap.
steps.why_this_step: Overtaking means the two vehicles are at the same absolute position, so the automobile must cover the gap plus the truck's own 60 m.

steps.text: Find the speed of each vehicle at this time using v = at.

final_answer.value: (a) t ≈ 7.39 s. (b) initial gap d ≈ 35.45 m. (c) v_truck ≈ 16.25 m/s, v_auto ≈ 25.85 m/s.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the truck's 60 m displacement itself as the initial gap between the vehicles, giving d = 60 m.
Using the automobile's own acceleration on the 60 m distance to find the time, 60 = ½(3.5)t², giving the wrong time t ≈ 5.86 s.

question.text: Water in a 400 m wide river moves downstream at a speed of 2.0 m/s. A boat travels at 10.0 m/s relative to the water, keeping its heading aligned perpendicular to the stream.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the duration required for the boat to arrive at the far bank.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Calculate the downstream distance between the boat's landing spot and the point located directly across from its launch position.

conditions: boat velocity relative to water = 10.0 m/s
heading is strictly perpendicular to current

solution.approach: The boat's velocity relative to water is perpendicular to the bank, so the crossing time depends only on that component, and the drift is the current speed times this time.

steps.text: The boat's velocity relative to water, 10.0 m/s, is entirely perpendicular to the river, since only the current carries it sideways.
steps.why_this_step: The perpendicular component alone determines how fast the boat closes the 400 m width.

steps.text: Find the time to cross by dividing the width by the perpendicular velocity.
During this time, the current carries the boat downstream at 2.0 m/s; multiply by the crossing time to get the drift.

common_mistakes.text: Using the resultant speed √(10.0² + 2.0²) = 10.2 m/s instead of only the perpendicular component gives a wrong time of about 39.2 s.
Swapping the roles of the two given speeds gives a drift of 400 × 10.0/2.0 = 2000 m, an unreasonably large value.

question.text: Explain why the kinematic expression sₜ = u + at − ½ a appears to be dimensionally inconsistent.
conditions: sₜ is distance traveled during the t-th second

solution.approach: Each term hides a factor of the one-second interval written as the bare number 1; restoring that factor shows the expression is dimensionally consistent.

steps.text: sₜ is the displacement during the t-th second, the interval between time t − 1 s and time t, found from the position formula s(τ) = uτ + ½aτ².
Expanding this difference and grouping terms gives every part of sₜ multiplied by a factor of the one-second interval, which the short form of the equation leaves unwritten.
steps.equation: sₜ = u(1 s) + ½a(1 s)(2t − 1 s)

steps.text: Check the dimension of each term: u(1 s) is a velocity times a time, a length; ½a(1 s)(2t − 1 s) is an acceleration times two time intervals, also a length.
steps.why_this_step: Once both time intervals are written out, every term on the right has the dimension of length, matching sₜ.

steps.text: Writing the 1 s factors as the bare number 1, as the short form does, gives sₜ = u + at − ½a; the formula looks unbalanced only because that unit has been dropped, not because it is wrong.
steps.equation: sₜ = u + at − ½a, with the 1 s factors suppressed

final_answer.value: The 1 s interval in each term is written as the bare number 1. Restoring it gives sₜ = u(1 s) + ½a(1 s)(2t − 1 s), where every term is a length, so the equation is dimensionally consistent once the suppressed unit is put back.

common_mistakes.text: Concluding the relation is dimensionally wrong outright, instead of noticing that its second and third terms carry a suppressed factor of 1 s that restores their dimension of length.

question.text:
Assertion: For two particles traveling along a straight path, the displacements vary with time as s₁ = 2t − 4t² and s₂ = − 2t + 4t². The relative velocity between them continually increases.
Reason: An object's speed grows whenever its velocity and acceleration have the same sign.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

solution.approach: Differentiate both displacement equations to get the relative velocity and relative acceleration, then check their signs at t = 0.

steps.text: Differentiate each displacement equation to get the two velocities.
Find the relative velocity of particle 1 with respect to particle 2.
Differentiate again to get the relative acceleration, which is constant.
At t = 0, v_rel = +4 and a_rel = −16 have opposite signs, so by the Reason's own rule the relative speed decreases at first instead of increasing throughout.
The Assertion is therefore false, while the Reason states a true general rule about velocity and acceleration signs.

final_answer.value: Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Seeing a nonzero constant relative acceleration and assuming the relative speed must keep increasing, without checking the signs of v_rel and a_rel at t = 0, wrongly marks both statements true.

question.text: A pair of diamonds are released from rest at an identical elevation, one falling 1.0 s after the other. Find the time elapsed since the release of the initial diamond at which the vertical gap separating the two stones reaches 10 m. (Use g = 10 m/s²)
conditions: released from the same initial height

solution.approach: Write the distance fallen by each diamond as a function of time from the first diamond's release, then set the gap between them to 10 m to find that time.

steps.text: Measure time t from when the first diamond is released. Its distance fallen is ½gt².
The second diamond is released 1.0 s later, so for t ≥ 1 s its distance fallen is ½g(t − 1)².
The gap between them, for t ≥ 1 s, is the difference of these two distances.
Set the gap to 10 m and solve for t.

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring that the second diamond is already falling and solving 5t² = 10 for the gap gives t = √2 ≈ 1.41 s; the distance fallen since t = 1.0 s must be subtracted.

question.text: The variation of velocity with time for a body executing one-dimensional motion is depicted in the given diagram. The body starts from an initial position of s = −10 m at t = 0 s. Draw the corresponding acceleration-time (a-t) and displacement-time (s-t) graphs for the entire interval from t = 0 s to t = 10 s.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Plot the acceleration-time (a-t) graph for the interval t = 0 s to t = 10 s.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Plot the position-time (s-t) graph for the interval t = 0 s to t = 10 s.

conditions: at t = 0 s, position s = −10 m
from t = 0 s to t = 2 s, velocity increases linearly from 0 m/s to 10 m/s
from t = 2 s to t = 4 s, velocity remains constant at 10 m/s
from t = 4 s to t = 8 s, velocity decreases linearly from 10 m/s to −10 m/s (crossing 0 m/s at t = 6 s)
from t = 8 s to t = 10 s, velocity increases linearly from −10 m/s to 0 m/s

figure.description: A velocity versus time (v-t) graph displaying piecewise linear segments from t = 0 s to t = 10 s. The velocity starts at (0 s, 0 m/s), increases linearly to (2 s, 10 m/s), remains flat at 10 m/s until (4 s, 10 m/s), drops linearly through (6 s, 0 m/s) to reach a minimum of −10 m/s at (8 s, −10 m/s), and finally rises linearly to end at (10 s, 0 m/s).

solution.approach: Read the slope of each straight segment of the v-t graph for acceleration, and add the signed area under v-t to the initial position for the s-t graph.

steps.text: Find acceleration on each segment as the slope of the v-t line; the acceleration graph is a step function.
Start the position at s = −10 m at t = 0 and add the area under v-t up to each breakpoint.
Between breakpoints, the s-t graph is a parabola while v is changing, and a straight line while v is constant.
steps.equation: s(t) = −10 + 2.5t² for 0≤t≤2 s; s(t) = 10t − 20 for 2≤t≤4 s; curved between 4 and 8 s with a peak s = 30 m at t = 6 s (where v = 0); curved between 8 and 10 s
steps.why_this_step: The s-t curve bends wherever v itself is changing, and is straight only while v is constant.

final_answer.value: a-t graph: a = 5 m/s² from t = 0–2 s, a = 0 from t = 2–4 s, a = −5 m/s² from t = 4–8 s, a = 5 m/s² from t = 8–10 s (a step graph). s-t graph passes through (0,−10), (2,0), (4,20), (6,30) [peak, since v = 0 here], (8,20), (10,10) m — a rising parabola from t = 0–2 s, a straight rising line from t = 2–4 s, and parabolic curves from t = 4–8 s and t = 8–10 s.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the s-t graph as straight lines between every pair of breakpoints instead of a curve wherever the velocity is itself changing.
Missing that acceleration is zero during the constant-velocity segment from t = 2 s to t = 4 s, and drawing a nonzero acceleration there instead.

concept_tags: s-t graph from area under v-t

question.text: The velocity-displacement (v-s) curve of a particle executing rectilinear motion is a straight line with a non-zero positive y-intercept and a positive slope. Sketch the corresponding acceleration-displacement (a-s) graph.
conditions: velocity v depends linearly on displacement s
positive rate of change dv/ds (positive slope)

figure.description: A graph with displacement s plotted along the horizontal axis and velocity v along the vertical axis shows a straight line located in the first quadrant, starting from a positive value on the vertical axis and rising with a positive slope.

solution.approach: Write the v-s line as an equation, use a = v dv/ds to get acceleration as a function of s, and read off its intercept and slope.

steps.text: Write the given straight-line v-s graph as an equation with a positive intercept c and a positive slope m.
Use the identity that relates acceleration to velocity and displacement.
The slope of the v-s line is constant, so dv/ds = m; substitute this and the expression for v.

This is again a straight line in s, with a positive intercept mc and a positive slope m², so the a-s graph is also a straight line with a positive intercept and a positive slope, matching the graph shown.
steps.equation: a-s line: intercept = mc, slope = m²

final_answer.value: a = mc + m²s, a straight line in s with positive intercept mc and positive slope m², matching the graph shown

common_mistakes.text: Using a = dv/dt directly with the v-s slope m as if it were a time rate gives a as a constant, missing that a depends on s through the v(dv/ds) relation.

question.text: A stream of water has a width of 20 m and flows at 3 m/s. A small boat moves with a speed of 2√2 m/s relative to the water, directed at an angle of 45° with respect to the downstream flow.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Calculate the time needed for the boat to reach the opposite side.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the distance from the point straight across from the initial position to where the boat arrives on the opposite bank.

conditions: boat speed relative to water = 2√2 m/s
direction of boat relative to river current = 45°

solution.approach: Resolve the boat's velocity relative to water across and along the river; the across part fixes the crossing time, and the along part adds to the current to fix drift.

steps.text: Resolve the boat's velocity relative to water, 2√2 m/s at 45° to the current, into components across and along the river.
steps.equation: v_across = 2√2 sin45° = 2 m/s, v_along = 2√2 cos45° = 2 m/s

steps.text: The crossing time depends only on the across component, since that is what closes the 20 m width.
The ground velocity along the river is the current plus the boat's own along-river component, since both point the same way.
The drift is this along-river ground velocity times the crossing time; state both results.

common_mistakes.text: Using only the current speed for the drift and ignoring the boat's own along-river component gives 30 m instead of 50 m.
Using the full boat speed 2√2 m/s instead of only its across-river component to find the crossing time gives 7.1 s instead of 10 s.

question.text: Ship A and ship B are initially separated by a distance of 10 km along a north-south axis, with ship A positioned to the north of ship B. Ship A moves due west at a constant speed of 20 km/h, while ship B sails due north at a constant speed of 20 km/h. Determine the shortest distance between the two vessels and the time taken to reach this minimum separation.
conditions: initial separation along north-south line = 10 km
ship A is north of ship B initially
velocity of ship A = 20 km/h due west (constant)
velocity of ship B = 20 km/h due north (constant)

solution.approach: Find the velocity of ship B relative to ship A, then find the shortest distance from A to the straight-line path that B follows relative to A.

steps.text: Set up coordinates with east and north as axes. Place B at the origin and A 10 km north of it, and write both velocities as vectors.
Find the velocity of B relative to A.
Find the position of B relative to A at t = 0.
steps.equation: r_BA(0) = B − A = (0, −10) km, that is, 10 km south of A

steps.text: Write the relative position as a function of time and minimize the squared distance from A (the origin of this relative frame).
Differentiate the squared distance and set it to zero to find the time of closest approach.
Substitute t = 0.25 h back to get the minimum distance.

final_answer.value: distance of closest approach = 5√2 km ≈ 7.07 km, reached after 0.25 h = 15 minutes

common_mistakes.text: Using the initial separation of 10 km directly as the closest approach, without accounting for the relative motion, misses that the two ships close in further before moving apart.
Adding the two speeds as 20 + 20 = 40 km/h for the relative speed instead of combining them as perpendicular vectors gives a wrong relative velocity of 40 km/h instead of 20√2 km/h.

question.text: An elevator is traveling upwards while slowing down. State the respective directions of its velocity and acceleration at this moment.

solution.approach: Ascending fixes the direction of velocity as upward; a decreasing speed while moving in that direction means the acceleration opposes the velocity.

steps.text: The lift is ascending, so its velocity is directed upward.
Its speed is decreasing while it moves upward, so the net force and acceleration must act opposite to the velocity.
State both directions.

final_answer.value: Velocity is directed upward; acceleration is directed downward.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the acceleration also points upward because the lift is going up, ignoring that its speed is decreasing.

question.text: A body initially at rest is located at the position (2 m, 4 m) when t = 0. It begins to travel with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s² directed along the positive x-axis. After a duration of 2 s, another constant acceleration of magnitude 4 m/s² acts on it along the negative y-axis while the original x-acceleration continues. For a time instant 2 s later, determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: velocity of the particle

parts.label: b
parts.asks: coordinates of the particle

conditions: initial position is (2 m, 4 m) at t = 0
uniform acceleration along +x-direction of 2 m/s² for all t ≥ 0
additional uniform acceleration along −y-direction of 4 m/s² starting at t = 2 s

solution.approach: Track the x-motion over the full 4 s under its constant acceleration, and the y-motion only over the last 2 s once the second acceleration switches on.

steps.text: Find the x-velocity and x-displacement at t = 2 s, starting from rest with acceleration 2 m/s².
steps.equation: vₓ(2) = 4 m/s, x-displacement = 4 m, so x = 2 + 4 = 6 m

steps.text: The x-acceleration keeps acting for the next 2 s, so update x and vₓ over that interval too.
The y-acceleration of 4 m/s² in the negative direction acts only over the last 2 s, starting from v_y = 0.
Combine the x and y components for the velocity and the coordinates after the next 2 s.
steps.equation: (a) v = (8î − 8ĵ) m/s, |v| ≈ 11.3 m/s. (b) coordinates = (18 m, −4 m)

final_answer.value: (a) v = (8î − 8ĵ) m/s, magnitude ≈ 11.3 m/s. (b) coordinates = (18 m, −4 m)

common_mistakes.text: Restarting the x-motion at t = 2 s and ignoring the position and velocity built up in the first 2 s gives only 4 m of x-displacement in the next 2 s, not 12 m.
