question.text: A velocity-time plot for an automobile is a straight line that starts at the origin (0 s, 0 m/s) and passes through the point where velocity is 10 m/s at time t = 4 s. Based on this motion, calculate:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The acceleration of the automobile.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The total distance covered by the automobile in 8 s.

figure.description: A graph with time t (in s) on the horizontal axis and velocity v (in m/s) on the vertical axis. A straight line starts at (0, 0) and goes through the point (4, 10), extending steadily past t = 8 s.

solution.approach: Read the slope of the straight line for the acceleration, then use the area under the v-t graph for the distance travelled.

steps.text: Find the slope of the line using the origin and the marked point.
Find the velocity at t = 8 s using the same slope.
The distance travelled is the area under the v-t graph, a triangle from t = 0 to t = 8 s.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the area under the graph as a rectangle with height 20 m/s instead of a triangle gives 160 m instead of 80 m.

question.text: An object moves across the x-y plane. Initially, at t = 0, its position coordinates are (1 m, 2 m) and its velocity is (4î + 6ĵ) m/s. Later, at t = 4 s, it reaches the location (6 m, 4 m) with a velocity of (2î + 10ĵ) m/s. For this duration, determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the average velocity

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the average acceleration

parts.label: c
parts.asks: whether the average speed can be calculated using the provided information

conditions: initial position r₁ = (1 m)î + (2 m)ĵ at t₁ = 0
initial velocity v₁ = (4î + 6ĵ) m/s at t₁ = 0
final position r₂ = (6 m)î + (4 m)ĵ at t₂ = 4 s
final velocity v₂ = (2î + 10ĵ) m/s at t₂ = 4 s

solution.approach: Average velocity and average acceleration come from the change in position and velocity over the time interval; average speed needs the path length, which is not given.

steps.text: Divide the change in position by the 4 s interval for the average velocity.
Divide the change in velocity by the 4 s interval for the average acceleration.

Average speed needs the total path length travelled by the particle, and only its endpoints and instantaneous velocities there are known, not the actual curved path between them, so it cannot be found from this data.

final_answer.value: (a) average velocity = (1.25î + 0.5ĵ) m/s, magnitude ≈ 1.35 m/s. (b) average acceleration = (−0.5î + 1.0ĵ) m/s², magnitude ≈ 1.12 m/s². (c) No, average speed cannot be found from the given data because the actual path length travelled is unknown.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the magnitude of the average velocity vector, about 1.35 m/s, as the average speed wrongly assumes the particle moved in a straight line between the two points.

question.text: State two common examples of motion occurring in two dimensions.
conditions: motion restricted to a two-dimensional plane

figure.description: Two diagrams are shown: the first illustrates a closed circular path labeled 'Circular motion', and the second depicts a curved parabolic trajectory on an x-y coordinate frame labeled 'Projectile motion'.

solution.approach: Two-dimensional motion needs two coordinates to describe the path, such as the two motions shown in the figure.

steps.text: A particle moving on a circular path needs both x and y coordinates to describe its position at every instant, so it is two-dimensional motion.
A projectile launched at an angle to the ground moves along a curved path in a vertical plane, also needing two coordinates.

final_answer.value: Circular motion and projectile motion are two examples of two-dimensional motion.

question.text: The position (x) as a function of time (t) for a body constrained to travel along a straight line is described as follows: from t = 0 to 4 s, the position is steady at x = 4 m; between t = 4 s and t = 10 s, it decreases at a steady rate, passing through x = 0 at t = 6 s to reach x = −8 m at t = 10 s; from t = 10 s to t = 14 s, it increases at a constant rate until reaching x = 0 at t = 14 s. Construct the corresponding velocity-time (v-t) plot for this interval.

figure.description: An x-t graph showing position x (in meters) on the vertical axis against time t (in seconds) on the horizontal axis. The graph consists of three straight-line segments: a horizontal line at x = 4 m from t = 0 to 4 s; a downward sloping line connecting (4 s, 4 m) through (6 s, 0 m) to (10 s, −8 m); and an upward sloping line connecting (10 s, −8 m) to (14 s, 0 m).

solution.approach: Find the slope of each straight segment of the x-t graph; that slope is the constant velocity for the corresponding v-t segment.

steps.text: From t = 0 to 4 s, x stays constant at 4 m, so the slope, and hence the velocity, is zero.
From t = 4 to 10 s, x falls in a straight line from 4 m to −8 m, so the velocity is the constant slope of that line.
From t = 10 to 14 s, x rises in a straight line from −8 m to 0, so the velocity is the constant slope of that line.
The v-t graph is therefore three horizontal steps: v = 0 from 0 to 4 s, v = −2 m/s from 4 to 10 s, v = 2 m/s from 10 to 14 s.
steps.equation: v(t): 0 m/s, then −2 m/s, then 2 m/s

final_answer.value: v = 0 for 0–4 s, v = −2 m/s for 4–10 s, v = 2 m/s for 10–14 s

common_mistakes.text: Reading the middle segment's velocity using the crossing point at t = 6 s instead of the interval from 4 to 10 s gives the same slope but a shortened interval on the v-t plot.
Giving the last segment's velocity as −2 m/s by keeping the sign of the previous segment instead of recomputing the slope, which is actually positive.

question.text: A particle moves such that its instantaneous velocity is v = (2î − 4ĵ) m/s while its acceleration is given by a = (−2î + 4ĵ) m/s². What kind of motion does the particle undergo?

solution.approach: Compare the directions of v and a component by component; if acceleration always stays exactly along the same line as velocity, the path is a straight line.

steps.text: Compare the components of a with the components of v.
Since a is exactly opposite to v along the same line, and both are constant, the particle never gains a velocity component perpendicular to its original line of motion.
steps.equation: v and a lie on the same straight line at every instant

steps.text: Acceleration directly opposite to the velocity means the particle is slowing down along that line; it is a one-dimensional (straight-line) motion, not a curved path.
steps.equation: motion is rectilinear with uniform retardation
steps.why_this_step: A cross product of v and a being zero confirms the two vectors are collinear, which is the condition for straight-line motion.

final_answer.value: Straight-line (rectilinear) motion with uniform retardation, since the acceleration is constant and directed exactly opposite to the velocity.

common_mistakes.text: Seeing that both v and a have nonzero components in two directions and concluding the path must be two-dimensional (curved), without checking that a is a scalar multiple of v.

question.text: A body moves along a straight path such that its acceleration varies with time t according to the relation a = bt, where b is a constant. If the body sets off from the origin with an initial velocity v₀ at t = 0, find the total distance covered by it in time t.
conditions: motion along a straight line in one direction

solution.approach: Integrate the given acceleration once to get velocity as a function of time, then integrate again to get the distance travelled.

steps.text: Integrate the acceleration a(t) = bt to find the velocity, using the initial velocity v₀ as the constant of integration.
steps.equation: v(t) = v₀ + ∫₀ᵗ bt′ dt′ = v₀ + ½bt²

steps.text: Integrate the velocity to find the distance travelled, starting from the origin.

common_mistakes.text: Dropping the factor of one-half when integrating acceleration, using v(t) = v₀ + bt² instead of v₀ + ½bt², which on integrating gives v₀t + 1/3 bt³.
Misreading the increasing acceleration bt as a constant rate b, so using v(t) = v₀ + bt for the velocity, which on integrating gives v₀t + 1/2 bt².

question.text: A particle moves within the xy-plane such that its velocity at time t is given by v = (2t î + 3t² ĵ) m/s. Initially, at t = 0, it is located at the point (2 m, 4 m). Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the acceleration vector of the particle at t = 1 s.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the position vector and the coordinates of the particle at t = 2 s.

conditions: initial position at t = 0 is (2 m, 4 m)

solution.approach: Differentiate the velocity components to get acceleration, and integrate them using the given starting coordinates to get position.

steps.text: Differentiate each velocity component with respect to time.
steps.equation: v = 2t î + 3t² ĵ, a = dv/dt = 2î + 6t ĵ

steps.text: Substitute t = 1 s into the acceleration equation.
Integrate each velocity component with respect to time, using the starting coordinates (2 m, 4 m) as the constants of integration.
Substitute t = 2 s to get the position vector and coordinates.

final_answer.value: (a) a(1 s) = (2î + 6ĵ) m/s²; (b) r(2 s) = (6î + 12ĵ) m, coordinates (6 m, 12 m)

common_mistakes.text: Integrating 3t² as t³/3 instead of t³ gives y(2) = 6.67 m instead of 12 m.
Forgetting to add the starting coordinates 2 and 4 gives the position (4 m, 8 m) instead of (6 m, 12 m).

question.text: A body moves along a straight path covering the initial half of its total path length at a constant speed v₁. For the remaining half of the path length, it travels with a uniform speed v₂ for one-third of the duration taken for this half, and with a uniform speed v₃ for the other two-thirds of that duration. Determine the average speed of the body across the entire journey.
conditions: first half of total distance covered at constant speed v₁
for the second half distance, speed is constant at v₂ for 1/3 of the time taken
for the remaining 2/3 of the time taken for the second half, speed is constant at v₃

figure.description: A line segment AB representing the entire journey of distance 2d is split at point C into two equal lengths of distance d. Segment AC is traversed at speed v₁. Segment CB is split at point D such that the duration for CD is t/3 with speed v₂ and the duration for DB is 2t/3 with speed v₃.

solution.approach: Split the journey into the first half distance and the second half distance, find the time for each part, then divide the total distance by the total time.

steps.text: Let the total distance be 2d; the first half distance d is covered at speed v₁.
In the second half distance d, a time t splits into 1/3 of t at v₂ and 2/3 of t at v₃, and the distance covered equals d.
Solve this equation for t in terms of d, v₂ and v₃.
Add the two times and divide the total distance 2d by the total time.
Cancel d and simplify to the final expression.

common_mistakes.text: Treating v₂ and v₃ as covering equal distances instead of the stated time fractions, which changes the time split and gives a different, incorrect expression.

question.text: A vehicle completes a journey lasting a total of 60 min. For the initial 18 min, it moves with a mean speed of 11 ms⁻¹. In order to achieve an overall mean speed of 21 ms⁻¹ throughout the whole journey, determine the required mean speed over the remaining 42 min.
conditions: average speed in first interval = 11 ms⁻¹

solution.approach: Find the total distance needed for the whole trip's average speed, subtract the distance already covered, and divide by the remaining time.

steps.text: Convert the total trip time to seconds and find the total distance needed for an average speed of 21 m/s over the whole 60 min trip.
Find the distance covered in the first 18 min at 11 m/s.
Find the distance that must be covered in the remaining 42 min.
Divide this distance by the remaining time to get the required average speed.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the required speed is twice the target average speed minus the first-phase speed, using 2 × 21 − 11 = 31 ms⁻¹ instead of weighting by the actual times.

question.text: At time t = 0, an object begins moving from (0, 0) with an initial velocity of 8.0 ĵ m/s. Throughout its journey across the x-y plane, it experiences a uniform acceleration of (4.0 î + 2.0 ĵ) m/s². When the x-position of the object reaches 29 m, determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: its y-coordinate

parts.label: b
parts.asks: its speed

solution.approach: Use the x-motion to find the time when x = 29 m, then substitute that time into the y-motion and the velocity components.

steps.text: Write x(t) using zero initial x-velocity and aₓ = 4.0 m/s².
Set x(t) = 29 m and solve for t.
Write y(t) using initial y-velocity 8.0 m/s and a_y = 2.0 m/s², then substitute t.
Find the velocity components at this time and combine them for the speed.

common_mistakes.text: Writing x(t) = aₓt² instead of ½aₓt², dropping the one-half factor, gives t ≈ 2.69 s and y ≈ 28.8 m, both wrong.

question.text: A particle travels along a semicircular track having a radius of 1.0 m, starting at point A and reaching point B located at the opposite end of the diameter. If this motion takes a duration of 1.0 s, calculate the magnitude of the particle's average velocity.
conditions: points A and B are diametrically opposite ends of the path

figure.description: A semicircular path of radius 1.0 m connects starting position A at the top to final position B at the bottom along the circumference, with a straight vertical diameter of length 2.0 m joining A and B.

solution.approach: Average velocity depends only on the straight-line displacement between the start and end points, not on the curved path taken.

steps.text: Points A and B are the two ends of the vertical diameter of the semicircle.
The displacement from A to B is the diameter, twice the radius.
Divide the displacement by the time taken to get the average velocity.

common_mistakes.text: Using the curved arc length instead of the straight-line displacement gives π × 1.0 = 3.14 m/s, which is the average speed, not the average velocity.

question.text: The variation of velocity with time for a body executing one-dimensional motion is depicted in the given graph. Which of the following assertions is correct?

options.1: The particle's journey begins from the origin
options.2: The particle returns to its starting point at t = 2 s
options.3: The particle's mean speed during the duration 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s is zero

conditions: initial velocity v = 10 m/s at t = 0 s
velocity v = 0 m/s at t = 1 s

figure.description: A velocity–time (v–t) graph where velocity v (in m/s) is plotted along the vertical axis and time t (in s) along the horizontal axis. A single downward-sloping straight line connects the y-intercept at (0 s, 10 m/s), intersects the time axis at (1 s, 0 m/s), and extends into negative velocities, passing through (2 s, −10 m/s).

solution.approach: Read the velocity-time equation from the graph and use the area under it to check displacement and distance travelled over 0 to 2 s.

steps.text: The line passes through (0, 10) and (1, 0), so write velocity as a function of time.
The displacement from t = 0 to t = 2 s is the signed area under the graph. Compute it.
A zero displacement over this interval means the particle returns to its position at t = 0, so it crosses its initial position at t = 2 s.
steps.why_this_step: This holds whatever the particle's actual starting position is; the v-t graph alone does not say whether that position is the origin.

steps.text: Check the distance travelled, which is different from displacement since the velocity changes sign at t = 1 s. Add the magnitudes of area from 0–1 s and 1–2 s.
steps.equation: 5 m + 5 m = 10 m, average speed = 10/2 = 5 ms⁻¹, not zero

steps.text: The particle crosses its initial position at t = 2 s, which is the correct statement.

final_answer.value: The particle crosses its initial position at t = 2 s

common_mistakes.text: Computing the average velocity (displacement/time = 0/2 = 0) and calling it the average speed, which is actually the total distance over time, 10/2 = 5 ms⁻¹.

question.text: An object having mass m is dropped from rest at an altitude h. The object collides elastically with the floor, causing its speed to stay unchanged while reversing its motion upward. Draw the curve showing how its kinetic energy varies with elapsed time until the object reaches back to its starting height.
conditions: elastic collision with the ground (no loss of kinetic energy)

solution.approach: Kinetic energy grows as the square of the falling speed, peaks at the elastic bounce, then falls the same way as the ball rises back to its starting height.

steps.text: While falling from height h, speed grows as v = gt, so kinetic energy grows as the square of time.
steps.equation: KE(t) = ½m(gt)² = ½mg²t², for 0 ≤ t ≤ t₁ = √(2h/g)

steps.text: At the ground, all the potential energy has become kinetic energy; the elastic collision reverses the velocity direction but keeps its magnitude.
steps.equation: KE(t₁) = mgh, unchanged immediately after the bounce
steps.why_this_step: An elastic collision with the ground conserves kinetic energy, so no energy is lost at the bounce.

steps.text: On the way up, the ball's speed is g(2t₁ − t), so kinetic energy falls back to zero as the ball returns to height h.
steps.equation: KE(t) = ½mg²(2t₁ − t)², for t₁ ≤ t ≤ 2t₁, total time 2t₁ = 2√(2h/g)

final_answer.value: KE(t) rises from 0 at t = 0 to a peak mgh at t = t₁ = √(2h/g), following KE = ½mg²t²; at the bounce it stays mgh (elastic collision, no energy lost), then falls back along the mirror-image curve KE = ½mg²(2t₁ − t)² to 0 at t = 2t₁ = 2√(2h/g), when the ball is back at its initial position. The graph is two upward-curving parabolic pieces meeting at a sharp peak mgh at t = t₁.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing kinetic energy as a straight line rising to mgh and falling back, instead of the curved shape that follows from constant acceleration.
Assuming energy is lost at the bounce and drawing the rebound peak kinetic energy lower than the peak reached on the way down, even though the collision is elastic.

question.text: A ball projected straight upward with an initial speed v₀ attains a peak altitude h. What initial speed is needed to make the ball attain three times this peak altitude?

solution.approach: Use the relation between launch speed and maximum height, and compare the speeds needed for height h and for height 3h.

steps.text: Write the relation between the launch speed and the maximum height reached.
Write the same relation for the new speed v′ that gives triple the height.
Divide the two equations to eliminate g and h.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming height is directly proportional to speed instead of to the square of the speed, and tripling the speed to 3v₀.

question.text: Answer the following conceptual questions about motion in kinematics:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Can an object experience an acceleration while maintaining an unchanging speed?

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Can a body travel along a curved trajectory when its acceleration is: (i) zero, (ii) constant, or (iii) variable?

solution.approach: Acceleration depends on the change of the velocity vector, so a change of direction alone, or a change of speed alone, can each produce it.

steps.text: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector, which has both a magnitude, the speed, and a direction.
(a) In uniform circular motion the speed stays constant, but the direction of velocity keeps changing, so the acceleration is not zero.
steps.why_this_step: A constant magnitude does not mean a constant vector.

steps.text: So the answer to (a) is yes: a body can accelerate while travelling at constant speed.
(b) A curved path means the direction of velocity keeps changing along the path, and a change of direction alone needs a nonzero acceleration, so zero acceleration cannot give a curved path.
A constant acceleration can still give a curved path when it is not always along the velocity, as in a body thrown at an angle under constant gravity, which follows a curved path.
steps.equation: a = constant (e.g. g, downward), path = curved

steps.text: A variable acceleration can also give a curved path, for example a body going around a curve at changing speed, so both constant and variable acceleration are possible on a curved path, but zero acceleration is not.
steps.why_this_step: Combines (a) and (b) into the complete answer.

final_answer.value: (a) Yes, for example uniform circular motion, where speed is constant but direction changes. (b) A curved path is not possible with zero acceleration; it is possible with constant acceleration, for example a body thrown at an angle under gravity, and with variable acceleration, for example a curve taken at changing speed.

common_mistakes.text: Answering no to part (a) by treating constant speed as meaning constant velocity, missing that direction can still change.
Assuming a curved path always needs a changing acceleration, missing that a constant acceleration not along the velocity, as under gravity, also curves the path.

question.text: The velocity of a body moving along a one-dimensional path depends on time as v = (10 + 2t + 3t²) in SI units. Determine the following:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The body's displacement relative to the mean position at instant t = 1 s, assuming its displacement at t = 0 is 20 m.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The expression representing its acceleration as a function of time.

solution.approach: Integrate the velocity equation to get the displacement equation using the given value at t = 0, then differentiate velocity to get acceleration.

steps.text: Integrate v with respect to time to get x, keeping the integration constant.
Use the given value x = 20 m at t = 0 to find C.
Write the full displacement equation and substitute t = 1 s.
Differentiate v with respect to time to get the acceleration-time equation.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the constant of integration and using x = t³ + t² + 10t gives x(1) = 12 m instead of 32 m.
Integrating v instead of differentiating it to find acceleration gives a wrong result for part (b).

question.text: A particle moves along a straight path. Its acceleration varies with time as depicted in the acceleration-time graph, where the acceleration rises uniformly from 0 at t = 0 to a maximum of 4 m/s² at t = 2 s, and then decreases linearly back to 0 at t = 4 s. Given that the particle has a velocity of 2 m/s at t = 0, calculate its velocity at the end of the fourth second.
conditions: particle travels in a straight line
initial velocity at t = 0 is 2 m/s
acceleration increases linearly from 0 m/s² at t = 0 to 4 m/s² at t = 2 s
acceleration decreases linearly from 4 m/s² at t = 2 s to 0 m/s² at t = 4 s

figure.description: An acceleration-time (a-t) graph showing a triangle. The horizontal axis is time t in seconds, with markings at 0, 2, and 4. The vertical axis is acceleration a in m/s², with a marking at 4. The curve goes linearly from (0, 0) to (2 s, 4 m/s²), and then linearly down to (4 s, 0).

solution.approach: The change in velocity equals the area under the acceleration-time graph, so add the initial velocity to the total area of the triangular graph.

steps.text: Split the triangular a-t graph into two triangles and find the area of each.
steps.equation: area (0 to 2 s) = ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 m/s, area (2 to 4 s) = ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 m/s

steps.text: Add the two areas to get the total change in velocity from t = 0 to t = 4 s.
Add the change in velocity to the initial velocity.

common_mistakes.text: Misreading the peak of the graph as 2 m/s² instead of 4 m/s² gives Δv = ½ × 4 × 2 = 4 m/s and a wrong answer of 6 m/s.
Forgetting to add the initial velocity of 2 m/s gives v(4 s) = 8 m/s instead of 10 m/s.

concept_tags: area under graph gives change in velocity

question.text: An object having a mass of 1 kg moves with an initial velocity of 2 m/s. For a duration of 1 s, an unchanging 2 N force is applied to it at a right angle to its original direction of motion. Determine the object's velocity and displacement when the 1 s interval ends.
conditions: applied force is perpendicular to initial velocity

figure.description: Two vector diagrams: (a) shows the velocity components, with horizontal initial velocity u = 2 m/s and vertical component a t = 2 m/s, resulting in velocity vector v at an angle α to the horizontal; (b) shows the displacement components, with horizontal displacement u t = 2 m and vertical displacement ½ a t² = 1 m, resulting in displacement vector s at an angle β to the horizontal.

solution.approach: Since the force is perpendicular to the initial velocity, treat the motion as two independent components: unchanged velocity along the original direction and accelerated motion along the perpendicular direction.

steps.text: Find the acceleration produced by the force.
steps.equation: a = F/m = 2/1 = 2 m/s², directed perpendicular to u

steps.text: The velocity along the original direction stays u, and the perpendicular component grows from zero.
Combine the two perpendicular components to get the resultant velocity.
Find the displacement along each direction.
steps.equation: s∥ = ut = 2 × 1 = 2 m, s⊥ = ½at² = ½ × 2 × 1² = 1 m

steps.text: Combine the two perpendicular displacements to get the resultant displacement.

final_answer.value: v = 2√2 m/s ≈ 2.83 m/s at 45° to the initial velocity; s = √5 m ≈ 2.24 m at about 26.6° to the initial velocity

common_mistakes.text: Adding the perpendicular components as plain numbers instead of combining them as perpendicular vectors gives v = 4 m/s instead of 2√2 m/s.
Using s⊥ = at² for the perpendicular displacement instead of ½at² gives 2 m instead of 1 m.

question.text: A body travels along the +x-axis such that its velocity varies with time according to the equation v = (40 − 10 t) m/s, where t is expressed in seconds. Given that the body starts at x = 0 when t = 0, determine the time(s) at which it is located at a distance of 60 m from the origin.

solution.approach: Integrate v = 40 − 10t to get the position x(t), then solve x(t) = 60 m and x(t) = −60 m for every non-negative time.

steps.text: Integrate the velocity to get the position, starting from x = 0 at t = 0.
The particle moves in the positive direction until v = 0 at t = 4 s, reaching a maximum x = 80 m, then moves back through the origin into negative x.
Solve x(t) = 60 m; the particle passes this point once going out and once coming back.
Solve x(t) = −60 m for the positive root, since the particle also reaches 60 m from the origin on the negative side.

common_mistakes.text: Stopping after finding t = 2 s and 6 s misses that the particle later reaches 60 m on the negative side too, at t = 4 + 2√7 s.

question.text: A person walks eastward at a speed of 3 m/s while raindrops fall straight down at a speed of 4 m/s. Determine the angle and orientation at which the person must tilt an umbrella to stay protected from the rain.
conditions: velocity of person = 3 m/s due east
velocity of rain = 4 m/s vertically downwards
umbrella held opposite to the relative velocity of rain with respect to the person

solution.approach: Find the velocity of the rain relative to the man by subtracting his velocity from the rain's velocity, and hold the umbrella along that direction.

steps.text: Write the rain's velocity and the man's velocity as vectors, taking east and vertically up as positive.
The velocity of the rain relative to the man is the rain's velocity minus the man's velocity.
This vector points west and downward, so the rain reaches the man from the east side, tilted from the vertical by an angle whose tangent is the ratio of the horizontal to vertical parts.
The man should hold the umbrella tilted 37° from the vertical, towards the east, the direction he is walking.

final_answer.value: Tilt the umbrella 37° from the vertical, towards the east

common_mistakes.text: Adding the man's velocity to the rain's velocity instead of subtracting gives a tilt towards the west instead of the east.
Using tan θ = 4/3 instead of 3/4 gives 53° instead of 37°.

question.text: From the roof of a 40 m tall building, an object is projected vertically upward at a speed of 10 m/s. Determine the total duration of flight before it reaches the ground below. Assume g = 10 m/s².

solution.approach: Take upward as positive from the top of the tower, write the displacement equation, and set it equal to the position of the ground.

steps.text: Write the displacement of the ball from the top of the tower as a function of time, taking upward as positive.
The ground is 40 m below the starting point, so set s(t) equal to −40 m.
Rearrange into a standard quadratic and solve for t.
Reject the negative time since it comes before the ball is thrown; the ball strikes the ground at t = 4 s.

common_mistakes.text: Counting only the trip up and back down to the top of the tower (1 s up, 1 s down), giving 2 s and missing the further fall to the ground.

question.text: A faucet fixed at a height of 5 m releases droplets of water at equal time gaps. At the exact moment the first droplet strikes the floor, the third droplet begins to fall. Determine the height of the second droplet above the floor at this specific moment. (Take g = 10 ms⁻²)
conditions: regular time intervals between successive drops

solution.approach: Find the fixed interval between drops from the first drop's fall time, then find how long the second drop has fallen at the given instant.

steps.text: The first drop falls 5 m from rest, so find the time it takes to reach the ground.
Drops leave the tap at equal intervals T. When drop 3 leaves, drops 1 and 2 already left, so two intervals separate drop 1's release from drop 3's release, and that equals drop 1's fall time.
At this instant, drop 2 has been falling for one interval T = 0.5 s. Find the distance it has fallen.
Subtract this fallen distance from the tap height to get the height above the ground.

common_mistakes.text: Stopping after finding the distance the second drop has fallen (1.25 m) and reporting that as the height above the ground, instead of subtracting it from 5 m.

question.text: Starting from a stationary state, an automobile speeds up with a uniform acceleration α for a certain duration. Immediately afterward, it slows down with a uniform retardation β until it stops completely. Given that the entire motion takes t seconds, determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the highest speed attained by the automobile

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the overall distance covered during the journey

conditions: total time elapsed is t seconds

figure.description: A velocity-time (v-t) graph shaped like a triangle. The graph begins at the origin (0, 0), rises with a constant slope α for a duration t₁ to reach the maximum velocity v_max at point A, and subsequently drops with a constant slope −β over a duration t₂ to hit the time axis at point B, where the total time is t = t₁ + t₂.

solution.approach: The car reaches the same peak velocity at both phase boundaries; equate the two phase times to total time for peak velocity, then use the v-t triangle's area for distance.

steps.text: Let the accelerating phase last t₁ and the decelerating phase last t₂, reaching the same peak velocity v_max in both.
steps.equation: v_max = αt₁ = βt₂, so t₁ = v_max/α and t₂ = v_max/β

steps.text: Use the total time to connect the two phase times.
steps.equation: t₁ + t₂ = t → v_max/α + v_max/β = t

steps.text: Solve for the maximum velocity.
The v-t graph is a triangle of base t and height v_max, so the total distance is its area.
steps.equation: distance = ½ × t × v_max = ½ × t × αβt/(α + β) = αβt²/[2(α + β)]

final_answer.value: (a) v_max = αβt/(α + β); (b) total distance = αβt²/[2(α + β)]

common_mistakes.text: Adding α and β directly and writing v_max = (α + β)t instead of solving the two time equations together gives a completely wrong expression.
Using distance = v_max × t for the whole trip instead of half of it, since the motion is not at constant velocity, doubles the correct answer.

question.text: An object travels along a circular path having a radius R = 21/22 m at a uniform speed of 1 m/s. Over a time span of 2 s, determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the magnitude of its average velocity

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the magnitude of its average acceleration

solution.approach: Find the arc length in 2 s and the angle it subtends, then use it for the chord length (average velocity) and the change in velocity direction (average acceleration).

steps.text: The speed is constant at 1 ms⁻¹, so the arc length covered in 2 s is 2 m.
Find the angle this arc subtends at the centre, using the radius R = 21/22 m.
The displacement is the chord joining the start and end points, which depends on this angle.
Divide the chord length by the time for the average velocity.
The speed stays 1 ms⁻¹ throughout, but its direction turns through 120°, so the change in the velocity vector has magnitude 2v sin(θ/2); dividing by time gives the average acceleration.

final_answer.value: (a) magnitude of average velocity ≈ 0.83 ms⁻¹, (b) magnitude of average acceleration = √3/2 ≈ 0.87 ms⁻²

common_mistakes.text: Dividing the arc length by time instead of the chord length gives 1 ms⁻¹, which is the constant speed, not the average velocity.
Using the instantaneous centripetal acceleration v²/R = 22/21 ≈ 1.05 ms⁻² in place of the average acceleration over the 2 s interval.

question.text: A balloon moves vertically upwards with an acceleration a. When a stone is let go from this balloon, find the acceleration experienced by the stone immediately following its detachment.
conditions: balloon accelerates upward with acceleration a
stone is released from rest relative to the balloon
acceleration due to gravity is g downward

solution.approach: Once the stone is released it is a free body, and only gravity acts on it from that instant, regardless of the balloon's motion.

steps.text: Before release the stone shares the balloon's velocity, but not the cause of the balloon's acceleration.
At the instant of release, the only force acting on the stone is its own weight.
Apply Newton's second law to find the stone's acceleration immediately after release.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the stone keeps the balloon's upward acceleration a even after release, confusing continuity of velocity with continuity of acceleration.
Adding the balloon's acceleration to gravity as if the balloon still pushes the stone after separation, giving (g + a) downward.

question.text: A sphere is projected straight up into the air from ground level. Let T₁ represent the duration of its ascent to the highest point and T₂ represent the duration of its return to the ground. If air drag is taken into consideration throughout the motion, which relation is correct?
conditions: motion in a vertical line under gravity
T₁ is the time of ascent
T₂ is the time of descent

solution.approach: With air resistance, the effective deceleration going up is larger than g, and the effective acceleration coming down is smaller than g, so the times are unequal.

steps.text: Going up, both gravity and air resistance act downward, opposing the upward motion.
Coming down, gravity acts downward but air resistance acts upward, opposing the downward motion.
A larger deceleration going up brings the ball to rest sooner, while a smaller net acceleration coming down means it takes longer to return to the ground.

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring air resistance and assuming the upward and downward motions are symmetric, giving T₁ = T₂.

question.text:
The variation of velocity with respect to time for an object moving along the x-axis is presented in the graph. Calculate:
(a) the acceleration,
(b) the total distance covered between t = 0 and t = 10 s, and
(c) the displacement between t = 0 and t = 10 s.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: acceleration

parts.label: b
parts.asks: distance travelled in 0 to 10 s

parts.label: c
parts.asks: displacement in 0 to 10 s

conditions: initial velocity at t = 0 is 2 m/s
velocity at t = 10 s is 8 m/s

figure.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph plotting velocity v (in m/s) on the vertical axis against time t (in s) on the horizontal axis. The vertical axis has tick marks at 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 m/s. The horizontal axis is marked at 0, 5, and 10 s. A single continuous straight line starts at (t = 0 s, v = 2 m/s) and ends at (t = 10 s, v = 8 m/s).

solution.approach: Read the slope of the line for the acceleration, then use the area under the v-t graph, a trapezoid, for the distance, which equals the displacement here.

steps.text: Find the slope of the line using its two endpoints.
The distance travelled is the area under the v-t graph, a trapezoid with parallel sides 2 m/s and 8 m/s and width 10 s.
The velocity is positive throughout, so the displacement equals the distance travelled.

question.text: An object travels along a linear path experiencing uniform acceleration. Suppose it covers distances x, y, and z in the pth, qth, and rth seconds of its motion, respectively. Show that (q − r)x + (r − p)y + (p − q)z = 0.
conditions: distance covered in pth second is x
distance covered in qth second is y
distance covered in rth second is z

solution.approach: Write x, y, z using the distance-in-the-nth-second formula, substitute into the given combination, and show it collects into two brackets that both vanish.

steps.text: The distance covered in the nth second of motion with constant acceleration a and initial velocity u is this.
Write x, y, z using this formula for n = p, q, r.
steps.equation: x = u + a(p − ½), y = u + a(q − ½), z = u + a(r − ½)

steps.text: Substitute into the given combination and group the u terms and the a terms separately.
The coefficient of u is zero because the three bracketed terms cancel in pairs.
Expand the coefficient of a; every term in p, q, r of degree two cancels, and the remaining constant terms also cancel, leaving zero.
steps.why_this_step: With both brackets zero, the whole expression (q−r)x+(r−p)y+(p−q)z equals zero, which is what was to be proved.

final_answer.value: (q − r)x + (r − p)y + (p − q)z = 0, proved by substituting the nth-second distance formula for x, y, z and showing both the u-coefficient and the a-coefficient vanish.

common_mistakes.text: Using the total distance formula sₙ = un + ½an² instead of the distance-in-the-nth-second formula sₙ = u + a(n − ½) leads to an expression that does not reduce to zero.

question.text: The variation of the velocity of a particle with time is represented in the given v–t graph. Between t = 0 and t = 40 s, the graph forms two identical triangular lobes: it starts from rest at t = 0, increases linearly to a maximum of 5 m/s, returns linearly to 0 at t = 20 s, then drops linearly to a minimum of −5 m/s before increasing linearly back to 0 at t = 40 s. Determine:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The total distance covered by the particle in the first 40 s.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The average velocity of the particle throughout this 40 s duration.

conditions: peak positive velocity is 5 m/s between t = 0 and t = 20 s
minimum negative velocity is −5 m/s between t = 20 s and t = 40 s
velocity returns to 0 at t = 40 s

figure.description: A velocity-time (v–t) graph with velocity v on the vertical axis and time t in seconds on the horizontal axis. A triangular wave starts at the origin (0, 0), rises to a peak velocity of 5 m/s, and descends linearly to touch the time axis at t = 20 s. From t = 20 s, it continues downward linearly to a trough of −5 m/s, and then rises linearly to meet the time axis again at t = 40 s.

solution.approach: The area under a velocity-time graph gives distance and net displacement, so split the graph into its two triangular parts and combine them.

steps.text: The graph forms two triangles: velocity is positive from 0 to 20 s, reaching a peak of 5 m/s, and negative from 20 to 40 s, reaching a minimum of −5 m/s.
steps.equation: base = 20 s, height = 5 m/s for each triangle

steps.text: Find the area of the first triangle, the distance covered while the velocity is positive.
Find the area of the second triangle, the distance covered while the velocity is negative.
Total distance travelled is the sum of the magnitudes of both areas.
Net displacement is the signed sum: the positive area cancels the negative area, so the particle returns to its starting position.
steps.why_this_step: Displacement uses the sign of each area, not just its size, while distance adds the sizes.

steps.text: Average velocity is the net displacement divided by the total time; state both results.
steps.equation: Average velocity = 0 m / 40 s = 0 m/s; Distance = 100 m, Average velocity = 0 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Taking the net area (50 m − 50 m = 0) as the distance travelled gives 0 m instead of the correct 100 m.
Using only the first triangle's area as the total distance gives 50 m instead of 100 m.

question.text: An object is thrown straight up into the air with an initial speed of 40 m/s. Determine both the net displacement and the total distance covered by the object after the following time durations (take g = 10 m/s²):

parts.label: a
parts.asks: 2 s

parts.label: b
parts.asks: 4 s

parts.label: c
parts.asks: 6 s

solution.approach: Find the time to reach maximum height first; before that time distance equals displacement, and after it the distance adds the extra fall back down.

steps.text: Find the time to reach maximum height and the maximum height reached.
At t = 2 s the ball is still rising, since 2 s is less than 4 s, so find its position from the displacement equation.
Since the ball has not yet turned around, the distance travelled equals the displacement.
At t = 4 s the ball is exactly at the highest point, where displacement and distance are again equal.
steps.equation: (b) s(4) = 40(4) − 5(4)² = 80 m; displacement = 80 m, distance = 80 m

steps.text: At t = 6 s the ball has been falling back for 2 s after reaching the top at t = 4 s; find how far it fell in that time.
The distance travelled adds the rise and the fall, while the displacement is the net position from the start.
steps.equation: (c) distance = 80 + 20 = 100 m; s(6) = 40(6) − 5(6)² = 60 m, displacement = 60 m

common_mistakes.text: For part (c), taking the distance equal to the displacement, 60 m, and ignoring the extra distance covered while falling back down.

question.text: An object is thrown straight up into the air under gravity. State the acceleration of the object:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: as it travels upward,

parts.label: b
parts.asks: as it falls downward, and

parts.label: c
parts.asks: at the peak of its path.

solution.approach: Gravity acts on the particle the whole time it is in the air, so the acceleration stays g downward throughout, including at the highest point.

steps.text: Once the particle leaves the hand, the only force on it is its own weight, which acts vertically downward at every instant of the flight.
By Newton's second law the acceleration equals this force divided by the mass, so it is g downward regardless of whether the particle is moving up or down.
(i) During the upward journey the acceleration is g downward, opposing the upward velocity and slowing it down.
(ii) During the downward journey the acceleration is still g downward, now in the same direction as the velocity, speeding it up.
(iii) At the highest point the velocity is momentarily zero, but the force of gravity has not disappeared, so the acceleration there is also g downward, not zero.
steps.why_this_step: Acceleration depends on the net force, not on the instantaneous velocity, so a zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration.

final_answer.value: (a) g downward, (b) g downward, (c) g downward — the acceleration is g downward throughout the flight, including at the highest point

common_mistakes.text: Concluding the acceleration is zero at the highest point because the velocity is zero there, confusing zero velocity with zero acceleration.
Assuming the acceleration reverses direction between the upward and downward journeys, when in fact gravity acts downward the whole time and only the velocity's direction changes.

question.text: A particle moves with a velocity vector v = (2î + 3ĵ − 4k̂) m/s while experiencing zero acceleration. Determine whether the particle undergoes one-dimensional (1-D), two-dimensional (2-D), or three-dimensional (3-D) motion.

solution.approach: Zero acceleration keeps the velocity vector fixed in direction, so the particle travels along one straight line however many components its velocity has.

steps.text: The acceleration is zero, so the velocity vector never changes in magnitude or direction.
A velocity that never changes direction means the particle travels along a single fixed straight line in space.
A straight-line path is one-dimensional motion, regardless of how many axis components the velocity vector has.

common_mistakes.text: Calling it 3-D motion because the velocity vector has three nonzero components, instead of checking that its direction stays fixed.

question.text: At a given moment, the velocity vector of a moving particle is expressed as v = (3î + 4ĵ + 5k̂) m/s. Determine the particle's speed at this moment.
conditions: velocity vector is v = (3î + 4ĵ + 5k̂) m/s at the considered instant

solution.approach: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, found from the square root of the sum of the squares of its components.

steps.text: Write the velocity components along the three axes.
steps.equation: vₓ = 3 m/s, v_y = 4 m/s, v_z = 5 m/s

steps.text: Find the magnitude using the three-dimensional distance formula.
Simplify the square root to get the speed.

common_mistakes.text: Adding the three components directly instead of combining them as a vector, giving 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 m/s.
Leaving out the z-component and computing √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s.

question.text: The variation of acceleration with time for a body moving along a rectilinear path is displayed in the graph. At what time does the body regain its starting velocity?
conditions: acceleration a = 2 m/s² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 s
acceleration decreases linearly with time after t = 1 s, passing through a = 0 at t = 2 s
initial velocity is regained when total change in velocity is zero

figure.description: An acceleration-time (a-t) graph plotted on Cartesian axes with time t (in s) on the horizontal axis and acceleration a (in m/s²) on the vertical axis. From t = 0 to t = 1 s, the curve is a horizontal line at a = 2 m/s². From (1, 2), the graph continues as a straight line sloping downward with constant negative slope, crossing the horizontal axis at t = 2 s and continuing into the negative acceleration region.

solution.approach: The particle's velocity returns to its initial value when the net area under the a-t graph, from t = 0, becomes zero again.

steps.text: From t = 0 to 1 s, acceleration is constant at 2 m/s²; find the area, which is the change in velocity, for this part.
From t = 1 s to 2 s, acceleration falls linearly from 2 m/s² to 0; find this triangular area.
The total change in velocity up to t = 2 s is positive, so the particle has not returned to its initial velocity yet; for t > 2 s the acceleration keeps the same slope, going negative.
steps.equation: Δv(0 to 2 s) = 2 + 1 = 3 m/s; a(t) = 4 − 2t for t ≥ 1

steps.text: For a later time T, the extra area is a negative triangle of base (T − 2); set the total change in velocity to zero and solve for T.
steps.why_this_step: The velocity equals its initial value again exactly when the positive and negative areas under a-t cancel out.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the particle is back at its initial velocity when the acceleration itself reaches zero at t = 2 s, without checking that the area under a-t up to that point is not zero.
Ignoring the velocity change built up from t = 0 to 1 s, and solving only (T − 2)² = 1 for the negative triangle, giving the wrong time T = 3 s.

concept_tags: area under a-t gives change in velocity

question.text: A particle moves along a curve with its coordinates changing with time t as x = 5t and y = 2t² + t. Determine the time instant when its velocity is directed at 45° to the horizontal.
conditions: angle of velocity vector with horizontal = 45°

solution.approach: Differentiate x(t) and y(t) to get the velocity components, then set their ratio equal to tan 45°.

steps.text: Differentiate the position functions to get the velocity components.
A 45° angle with the horizontal means the two velocity components are equal.
Solve for t.

common_mistakes.text: Setting the ratio of the position coordinates y/x equal to 1 instead of the ratio of the velocity components, which gives t = 2 s.

question.text: To reach his farmland from his house, a cultivator walks 500 m towards the north, then 400 m towards the east, and finally 200 m towards the south. The entire journey takes a time of 20 min.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the total distance covered to reach the field.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine the net displacement vector from the house to the field.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Calculate the average speed of the cultivator during this journey.

parts.label: d
parts.asks: Calculate the average velocity of the cultivator during this journey.

conditions: displacement segments: 500 m north, 400 m east, 200 m south

solution.approach: Add the three legs of the walk for the distance, combine the north-south and east-west legs as vectors for the displacement, then divide each by the total time.

steps.text: Add the three legs walked to get the total distance.
Combine the two north-south legs: 500 m north and 200 m south leave a net 300 m north. The east leg stays 400 m east.
steps.equation: net north = 500 − 200 = 300 m, net east = 400 m

steps.text: Find the magnitude of the displacement using these two perpendicular components.
steps.equation: displacement = √(300² + 400²) = √250000 = 500 m, directed 53.1° east of north

steps.text: Convert 20 min to seconds and divide the distance by the time for the average speed.
Divide the displacement by the same time for the average velocity.
steps.equation: average velocity = 500/1200 = 5/12 ≈ 0.42 ms⁻¹, directed 53.1° east of north

final_answer.value: (a) distance walked = 1100 m, (b) displacement = 500 m, directed 53.1° east of north, (c) average speed = 11/12 ms⁻¹ ≈ 0.92 ms⁻¹, (d) average velocity = 5/12 ms⁻¹ ≈ 0.42 ms⁻¹, directed 53.1° east of north

common_mistakes.text: Reporting the average speed value, 0.92 ms⁻¹, as the average velocity, which confuses the total distance walked with the net displacement.

question.text: A train travels between two consecutive stops separated by a distance of 4 km in a total time of 4 min, beginning from rest at the first stop and coming to a halt at the second. If the motion consists first of a constant acceleration x followed immediately by a constant deceleration y, show that 1/x + 1/y = 2, where x and y are expressed in km min⁻².
conditions: initial phase has uniform acceleration x
second phase has uniform retardation y

solution.approach: Model the speed as a triangle on a velocity-time graph: its area gives the distance, its sides give the two times, linking x, y, T and D.

steps.text: The train starts from rest, accelerates at a uniform rate x to a maximum speed v, then retards at a uniform rate y to rest at the next station.
Add the two times; they must equal the total journey time T.
The distance covered is the area under the speed-time graph, a triangle of base T and height v.
Solve for v using the given distance and time.
Substitute this v into the time equation to get 1/x + 1/y.
steps.why_this_step: T/v is what v/x + v/y = T becomes after dividing both sides by v.

final_answer.value: 1/x + 1/y = 2, with x and y in km per minute squared

common_mistakes.text: Using D = vT instead of D = ½vT for the triangle area gives v = 1 km/min and 1/x + 1/y = 4, twice the correct value.

question.text: An elevator travels upward from rest, undergoing a constant acceleration a during the initial stage of its motion, followed by a constant deceleration of 2a until it comes to a complete stop. If the entire upward journey requires a total duration t, calculate the depth of the elevator shaft.
conditions: uniform upward acceleration a in the first stage
uniform upward deceleration 2a in the final stage
total time of ascent is t
motion is along a straight vertical line

solution.approach: Use that the lift reaches the same maximum speed at the end of both phases, split the total time t between phases using that condition, then add the two distances.

steps.text: Let t₁ be the time of uniform acceleration a and t₂ the time of uniform retardation 2a, with t₁ + t₂ = t. The maximum speed reached is the same seen from both phases.
Combine with t₁ + t₂ = t to find each time in terms of t.
Find the maximum speed and the distance covered while accelerating.
Find the distance covered while retarding from vₘₐₓ to rest.
Add the two distances to get the total depth of the shaft.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the acceleration phase and the retardation phase take equal time (t/2 each) instead of using the equal-maximum-speed condition, which gives at²/4.

question.text: At a specific moment, the velocity and acceleration vectors of a moving body are given by v = (3 î − 4 ĵ + 2 k̂) m/s and a = (2 î + ĵ − 2 k̂) m/s² respectively.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Calculate the scalar product v · a at this time.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Is the angle between vectors v and a acute, obtuse, or 90°?

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Determine if the speed of the body is increasing, decreasing, or staying constant at this time.

conditions: velocity v = (3 î − 4 ĵ + 2 k̂) m/s
acceleration a = (2 î + ĵ − 2 k̂) m/s²

solution.approach: Compute the dot product of v and a component by component, use its sign to classify the angle, and use the same sign for whether speed increases or decreases.

steps.text: Compute the dot product of v and a using their components.
The dot product is negative, and v·a = |v||a|cos θ with |v|,|a| both positive, so cos θ is negative.
steps.equation: cos θ < 0 ⟹ θ is obtuse (between 90° and 180°)

steps.text: The rate of change of speed equals the component of acceleration along the velocity direction, which is (v·a)/|v|. Since v·a is negative, this rate is negative.
steps.why_this_step: A negative rate of change of speed means the speed is decreasing at this instant.

common_mistakes.text: Mismatching components when computing the dot product, such as pairing the k̂ component of v with the ĵ component of a, gives a wrong value that can wrongly suggest an acute angle and increasing speed.

question.text: A body moves along a path such that the initial half of the total distance is covered at a uniform speed v₁ and the remaining half is covered at a uniform speed v₂. Determine the average speed of the body for the entire trip.
conditions: first half of total distance covered at constant speed v₁
second half of total distance covered at constant speed v₂
motion along a straight line path

solution.approach: Average speed is total distance divided by total time; find the time for each half from its distance and speed, then combine.

steps.text: Let the total distance be 2d, so each half of the journey covers distance d.
Find the time taken for each half from time = distance divided by speed.
Average speed is total distance over total time.
Cancel d and simplify to the standard form.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the plain arithmetic mean (v₁+v₂)/2, which is only correct when the two halves take equal time, not equal distance.

question.text: An aeroplane has a speed of 400 km/h relative to calm air. A steady wind blows toward the north at a rate of 200√2 km/h. To reach a destination B located 1000 km directly northeast of the starting position A, determine the heading angle the pilot needs to maintain and calculate the total duration required for the flight.
conditions: speed of aircraft in still air = 400 km/h
target point B is directly north-east of starting point A (45° north of east)

figure.description: A vector diagram with origin A. Vector v_w with magnitude 200√2 km/h points due north from A to C. The resultant velocity vector v_a points along the north-east direction (45° east of north) from A toward B. The relative velocity vector v_aw with magnitude 400 km/h goes from C to B, forming an angle α with the line AB.

solution.approach: Add the wind velocity and the aircraft's velocity relative to the wind as vectors, using a triangle where their sum points along AB, then solve for missing side and angle.

steps.text: Set up the vector triangle: the wind velocity from A to C, the aircraft's velocity relative to the wind from C to B, and their sum, the resultant ground velocity, from A to B along the north-east direction.
steps.equation: AC = 200√2 km/h, CB = 400 km/h, angle A = 45°

steps.text: Use the sine rule with the side opposite angle A being CB, to find the angle at B.
The remaining angle of the triangle gives the angle at C, and the sine rule gives the resultant ground speed AB.
The angle α between the steered direction CB and the path AB equals the angle at B, so the pilot steers 30° east of the AB direction, that is, 75° east of north.
steps.equation: α = B = 30°, heading = 45° + 30° = 75° east of north

steps.text: The journey time is the distance divided by the resultant ground speed.

final_answer.value: Steer at 75° east of north (30° east of AB), journey time ≈ 1.83 h

common_mistakes.text: Adding the wind speed and aircraft speed directly as 400 + 200√2 to get the ground speed, ignoring the angle between them, gives a wrong resultant.
Steering directly along AB (45° from north) without correcting for the wind reaches a point other than B.

question.text: An object is launched straight upwards from ground level. As it ascends, a person looking out of a window situated at a height of 15 m observes it passing by with an upward speed of 10 ms⁻¹. What is the velocity of the object 3 s following its release? (Use g = 10 ms⁻²)

solution.approach: Use the window height and speed to find the launch speed, then check whether 3 s falls before or after the ball reaches its highest point.

steps.text: The ball moves upward past the window at 10 ms⁻¹ at a height of 15 m. Use this to find the launch speed u from the ground.
Find the time taken to reach the highest point.
Since 3 s is later than 2 s, the ball has already passed its highest point and is coming down. Find its velocity at t = 3 s using v = u − gt, keeping the upward direction positive.
A negative value with upward taken as positive means the ball is moving downward at 10 ms⁻¹.

common_mistakes.text: Computing v = 20 − 10(3) = −10 correctly but not checking that the ball has already passed the top, and reading the 10 ms⁻¹ as still moving upward.
Using the window speed 10 ms⁻¹ directly as the launch speed u instead of solving for u from the window height and speed, giving v = 10 − 10(3) = −20 ms⁻¹.

question.text: An open elevator ascends vertically with an instantaneous speed of 10 m/s while accelerating upward at a rate of 2 m/s². At this moment, a ball is thrown straight up with a speed of 20 m/s relative to the ground from the base of the elevator. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the following:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The time elapsed before the ball returns to the elevator floor.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The vertical displacement of both the elevator and the ball at that moment.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: The total distance covered by the ball during this duration.

conditions: initial upward velocity of lift = 10 m/s
constant upward acceleration of lift = 2 m/s²
initial upward velocity of ball relative to ground = 20 m/s
ball starts from lift floor at t = 0
acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s² downward

solution.approach: Write the displacement of the lift and of the ball as functions of time from the same starting point, and set them equal to find when they meet again.

steps.text: Write the lift's displacement, starting with an upward speed of 10 m/s and an upward acceleration of 2 m/s².
Write the ball's displacement, projected upward at 20 m/s and acted on only by gravity.
Set the two displacements equal and solve for t, keeping the positive, nonzero root.
Substitute t = 5/3 s into either displacement equation to get the common displacement at that instant.

Check the ball's velocity at this instant to see if it has already turned back; since it is still positive, the ball has travelled straight up the whole time, so the distance travelled equals its displacement.

final_answer.value: (a) t = 5/3 s ≈ 1.67 s, (b) both lift and ball at 175/9 m ≈ 19.4 m, (c) distance travelled by ball ≈ 19.4 m

common_mistakes.text: Taking t = 0 as the meeting time instead of discarding it as the starting instant, since both objects begin together at t = 0.
Assuming the ball has already reached its highest point by t = 5/3 s and using its full rise time of 2 s to compute distance, when it is in fact still rising.

question.text: A soccer ball is launched straight up into the air from ground level. As it ascends, an observer looking through a window located 15.0 m above the ground notes that the ball travels past with an upward speed of 5.00 m/s. Assume that air drag is negligible and use g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: What is the maximum height reached by the ball above the ground?

parts.label: b
parts.asks: What is the total time needed for the ball to rise from the ground to the peak of its trajectory?

conditions: speed at height 15.0 m is 5.00 m/s upward

solution.approach: Use v² = u² − 2gh between the ground and the window to find the launch speed, then find the maximum height and time to the top from that speed.

steps.text: Apply v² = u² − 2gh between the ground, where the speed is u, and the window, 15 m up, where the speed is 5.00 m/s.
Find the maximum height using v² = u² − 2gH with v = 0 at the top.
Find the time to the top using v = u − gt with v = 0 at the top.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the given 5.00 m/s as the ground launch speed and ignoring the 15 m window height gives a maximum height of only 1.25 m.

question.text: A body moves in a straight line along the x-axis. A position-time (x versus t) plot representing its motion is a straight line that intersects the vertical position axis at x = −20 m when t = 0 s, and crosses the horizontal time axis at t = 10 s when x = 0 m. Based on this information, analyze the motion by answering the following:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the initial location of the particle at t = 0 s.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Calculate the velocity of the particle.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Express the position x as a function of time t.

parts.label: d
parts.asks: State whether the motion has uniform or non-uniform velocity, and identify the time at which the object reaches the origin.

conditions: position-time graph is a straight line

figure.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing position x (in meters) along the vertical axis against time t (in seconds) along the horizontal axis. A single straight line with a constant positive slope passes through the points (t = 0 s, x = −20 m) and (t = 10 s, x = 0 m).

solution.approach: Read the starting position and the slope of the straight line x-t graph, and note that a constant slope means constant velocity.

steps.text: Read the position at t = 0 from the graph.
Find the slope of the line using the two given points.
State what the constant, positive slope means for the motion.
steps.why_this_step: A straight line on an x-t graph means constant velocity, so the particle moves with uniform motion in the positive x-direction.

steps.text: Read the time at which the particle crosses the origin.

final_answer.value: The particle starts at x = −20 m and moves with a constant velocity of +2 m/s (zero acceleration). The position as a function of time is x = x₀ + vt = (−20 + 2t) m, reaching x = 0 m at t = 10 s; it is in uniform motion in the positive x-direction throughout.

common_mistakes.text: Reading the y-intercept as the velocity instead of the slope gives a wrong velocity of −20 m/s.
Reading the intercept as +20 m instead of −20 m, ignoring its sign, gives the wrong starting position and the wrong equation x = 20 + 2t.

question.text: An object is projected vertically upward from the surface of the earth. Throughout its flight, a steady resistive force acts on it, causing a deceleration of magnitude 2 ms⁻². Taking g = 10 ms⁻², determine the ratio comparing the duration of upward motion to that of downward motion back to the ground.

solution.approach: The resistance adds to gravity on the way up and subtracts from it on the way down, so use the two accelerations to find each time and take the ratio.

steps.text: On the way up, both gravity and the resistance act downward, opposing the motion.
On the way down, the resistance acts upward, against gravity.
Write the time of ascent and the maximum height reached, for initial speed u.
Write the time of descent from that height using h = ½a_down t₂².
Divide the two times to get the ratio.
steps.why_this_step: The u cancels, so the ratio does not depend on the launch speed.

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the resistance force and using the same acceleration g for both ascent and descent gives a ratio of 1 : 1.
Inverting the ratio, computing time of descent to time of ascent instead, gives √(3/2).

question.text: A pair of balls, labeled A and B, are launched straight up into the air at unequal initial speeds. Determine the acceleration of ball A with respect to ball B during their free flight.

solution.approach: Both balls have exactly the same acceleration, g downward, at every instant, so their relative acceleration is the difference of two equal vectors.

steps.text: Write the acceleration of each ball; after leaving the hand, both are in free fall under gravity alone.
The initial velocities are different, but that does not affect the acceleration, which stays g downward for both balls at every instant.
steps.why_this_step: Relative acceleration compares accelerations, not velocities; the different launch speeds only give the balls different velocities, not different accelerations.

steps.text: Relative acceleration of A with respect to B is the difference of the two accelerations.

final_answer.value: Zero — the relative acceleration is zero because both balls fall under the same gravitational acceleration g throughout the motion.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the ball projected with the higher speed must also have a higher acceleration gives a wrongly nonzero relative acceleration.

question.text: For an object moving with a time-dependent velocity vector v, answer the following questions:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Explain the physical meaning conveyed by each of the two mathematical expressions |dv/dt| and d|v|/dt.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine whether there are situations in which these two quantities are equal to each other.

solution.approach: |dv/dt| is the size of the acceleration vector, while d|v|/dt is the rate at which only the speed changes; compare what each one includes to see when they can match.

steps.text: dv/dt is the acceleration vector, the rate of change of the velocity vector. Its magnitude |dv/dt| includes any change in the direction of velocity as well as any change in speed.
|v| is the speed, a single number with no direction. d|v|/dt is the rate of change of this number, so it tracks only a change in speed.
steps.equation: d|v|/dt = rate of change of speed

steps.text: When the acceleration is along the velocity, so that the object moves in a straight line with its speed increasing, the whole acceleration changes the speed and the two quantities are equal; if it moves in a straight line while slowing down, d|v|/dt is negative and equals −|dv/dt|.
steps.equation: speed increasing in a straight line: |dv/dt| = d|v|/dt; speed decreasing: d|v|/dt = −|dv/dt|

steps.text: In motion along a curved path, part of the acceleration changes only the direction, not the speed, so the two quantities are not equal in general; for example, in uniform circular motion the speed is constant, d|v|/dt = 0, but |dv/dt| = v²/R, which is not zero.
steps.equation: curved path, uniform circular motion: |dv/dt| = v²/R ≠ 0 = d|v|/dt

final_answer.value: |dv/dt| is the magnitude of the acceleration vector; d|v|/dt is the rate of change of speed. They are equal only when the acceleration is along the velocity, as in straight-line motion with increasing speed; they are not equal in general, as shown by uniform circular motion where d|v|/dt = 0 while |dv/dt| = v²/R ≠ 0, and by straight-line motion with decreasing speed where d|v|/dt = −|dv/dt|.

common_mistakes.text: Treating |dv/dt| and d|v|/dt as always equal because both are formed from the same velocity, missing that one is a vector magnitude and the other is a rate of change of a scalar.

question.text: The variation of velocity with time for an object traveling along a straight path is provided in the figure. Given that its position coordinate is s = 20 m at t = 0, construct the corresponding acceleration versus time (a-t) and position versus time (s-t) graphs for the entire motion.
conditions: velocity-time profile consists of linear segments from t = 0 to t = 14 s

figure.description: A plot of velocity v (m/s) versus time t (s) consisting of connected straight line segments: from t = 0 to 4 s, v remains constant at −20 m/s; from t = 4 to 6 s, v rises linearly from −20 m/s to 0 m/s; from t = 6 to 8 s, v falls linearly from 0 m/s to −20 m/s; from t = 8 to 12 s, v increases linearly from −20 m/s to +20 m/s, crossing v = 0 at t = 10 s; from t = 12 to 14 s, v decreases linearly from +20 m/s to 0 m/s.

solution.approach: Find acceleration as the slope of each straight segment of the v-t graph, then build the s-t graph by adding the signed area under v-t to the starting position.

steps.text: Find acceleration on each segment as the slope of the v-t line.
Start the position at s = 20 m at t = 0 and add the area under v-t up to each breakpoint.
Between breakpoints the s-t graph is straight while v is constant, and curved while v is changing linearly.
steps.equation: straight falling line for 0≤t≤4 s; curved between 4 and 12 s with a minimum s = −120 m at t = 10 s (where v = 0); curved between 12 and 14 s
steps.why_this_step: The minimum of the s-t graph occurs exactly where the velocity crosses zero.

final_answer.value: a-t graph: a = 0 from t = 0–4 s, a = 10 m/s² from t = 4–6 s, a = −10 m/s² from t = 6–8 s, a = 10 m/s² from t = 8–12 s, a = −10 m/s² from t = 12–14 s (a step graph). s-t graph passes through (0,20), (4,−60), (6,−80), (8,−100), (10,−120) [minimum, since v = 0 here], (12,−100), (14,−80) m — a straight falling line from t = 0–4 s, and curves elsewhere.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the particle keeps moving in the same direction throughout, instead of recognising the minimum position occurs at t = 10 s where the velocity is zero.
Drawing the s-t segment from t = 0 s to t = 4 s as a curve, when the velocity is constant there and the position actually falls in a straight line.

question.text: At the same instant, two bodies labeled 1 and 2 are launched vertically. Body 1 is released at an elevation of 20 m above the ground heading downward with a speed of 5 m/s, whereas body 2 is projected straight upward from ground level at 20 m/s. Treating the upward direction as positive, determine the following:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the acceleration of particle 1 relative to particle 2

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the starting velocity of particle 2 relative to particle 1

parts.label: c
parts.asks: the velocity of particle 1 relative to particle 2 at time t = ½ s

parts.label: d
parts.asks: the instant at which the two particles meet

conditions: initial height of particle 1 is 20 m
initial velocity of particle 1 is 5 m/s downwards
initial velocity of particle 2 is 20 m/s upwards

figure.description: A vertical diagram showing particle 1 at a height of 20 m above the ground moving downward with an arrow labeled 5 m/s, and particle 2 at the ground moving upward with an arrow labeled 20 m/s. An upward arrow indicates the positive (+ve) reference direction.

solution.approach: Both particles are in free fall, so they share the same acceleration; the relative motion between them is therefore at constant relative velocity, which gives all four parts directly.

steps.text: Both particles accelerate at g downward under gravity alone, so their relative acceleration is zero.
steps.equation: a₁ = a₂ = −g (upward positive) → a_(1/2) = a₁ − a₂ = 0

steps.text: Taking upward as positive, particle 1 starts moving down at 5 m/s and particle 2 starts moving up at 20 m/s; find the initial velocity of 2 relative to 1.
Since the relative acceleration is zero, the relative velocity of 1 with respect to 2 never changes from its initial value.
steps.why_this_step: A zero relative acceleration means the relative velocity stays constant for all time.

steps.text: With separation 20 m and a constant closing speed of 25 m/s, find the time to collide.

final_answer.value: (a) acceleration of 1 with respect to 2 = 0. (b) initial velocity of 2 with respect to 1 = 25 m/s (upward). (c) velocity of 1 with respect to 2 at t = ½ s = 25 m/s (downward), unchanged from t = 0. (d) time to collide = 0.8 s.

common_mistakes.text: Adding the two initial velocities instead of subtracting, giving an initial relative velocity of 20 + (−5) = 15 m/s.
Assuming the relative velocity changes with time and recomputing it at t = ½ s from the individual free-fall equations, instead of recognising that a zero relative acceleration keeps it constant.

question.text: An object moves with a uniform speed of 2 m/s for the first half of its total travel duration. Throughout the second half of the time, it covers ¼ of the distance traveled in that interval at a steady speed of 4 m/s, and the other ¾ of the distance at 6 m/s. Determine the average speed of the object over the entire journey.
conditions: motion for first half of total duration is at constant speed 2 m/s
motion for second half of total duration is split by distance: ¼ at 4 m/s and ¾ at 6 m/s

solution.approach: Write every distance in terms of the total time, add them up, and divide by the total time so the total time cancels out.

steps.text: Let the total time of the journey be T. In the first half of the time, T/2, the particle moves at 2 m/s.
In the second half of the time, T/2, the particle covers some distance d2, one quarter of it at 4 m/s and three quarters of it at 6 m/s; write the time for each part and add them to T/2.
Solve this equation for d2.
Add the two distances to get the total distance covered.
Average speed is total distance divided by the total time T, and T cancels out.
steps.why_this_step: Since every distance was written proportional to T, the actual value of T never matters.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the plain average of the three speeds, (2 + 4 + 6)/3 = 4 m/s, instead of weighting each speed by the time or distance it actually covers.
Reading the 1/4 and 3/4 split as a split of the second half's time rather than its distance, which gives an average speed of 3.75 m/s instead of 11/3 m/s.

question.text: A stone is thrown straight up from a high point A. When it is at a depth h beneath A, the speed of the stone is twice the speed it possessed at an elevation h over A. Prove that the stone reaches a maximum height of (5/3)h above point A.
conditions: stone projected vertically upward from point A
speed at distance h below A is twice the speed at height h above A

solution.approach: Write v² = u² − 2g(displacement) for points h above and below A, use the given speed ratio to solve for u², then find the greatest height.

steps.text: Let u be the speed of projection at A, taking upward as positive. At height h above A, the speed v₁ satisfies this.
At distance h below A, the displacement from A is −h, so the speed v₂ satisfies this.
The speed below A is double the speed above A, so square this relation and substitute.
Expand and solve for u².
The greatest height above A is reached when the speed is zero, given by H = u²/(2g). Substitute u².
steps.why_this_step: H = u²/(2g) follows from v² = u² − 2gH with v = 0 at the highest point.

final_answer.value: Greatest height above A, H = 5h/3, proved by solving u² = 10gh/3 from the given speed condition and substituting into H = u²/(2g).

common_mistakes.text: Writing the speed below A as v₂² = u² − 2gh instead of u² + 2gh gives u² − 2gh = 4(u² − 2gh), so u² = 2gh and height h instead of 5h/3.
